news.title: Donald Trump cancels trip to Bucs-Steelers NFL game this weekend hours after CNN revealed his plans
news.text:
Donald Trump has canceled plans to attend a second football game in as many weeks, according to a report. 

One week after being forced to back out of attending the SEC showdown between Georgia and Alabama, the President has reportedly canceled a trip to an NFL game. 

CNN reported on Tuesday afternoon that Trump was expected to attend the Week 6 clash between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium in Florida on Sunday. 

However, the President seemingly pulled a quick U-turn, with the outlet reporting a matter of hours later that he would no longer attend the game. 

The matchup would have marked the second Steelers game that Trump has been in the stands for in two years. 

He also attended the Steelers’ matchup against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium in 2024 during his Presidential campaign against Kamala Harris. Pittsburgh proved to be a crucial swing state for the Republican party in the election. 

The U-turn comes less than a week after Trump was also forced to scrap his visit to the college football game between Georgia and Alabama. 

The trip was cancelled due to the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 storm, which made landfall on the Alabama coast on Friday evening.

'Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!' Trump posted to his Truth Social account on October 9.

'Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia but, hopefully, the Game will go on despite the weather! I will be visiting both of those Teams at a later date.'

The southeast of the US has been ravaged by Hurricane Isaias after it hit last Friday night, leaving four people dead and others injured.

The monster storm hit the Florida Panhandle near Destin at around 8.30pm as a Category 2 hurricane, packing maximum sustained winds of 105mph. 

Just 30 minutes later, its winds had fallen to 85mph, but the storm continued to wreak havoc along the Gulf Coast.

The rivalry clash between the Bulldogs and the Crimson Tide still went ahead in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, with the President missing out on a thrilling game. 

Georgia emerged as 20-17 winners at Bryant-Denny Stadium after a controversial finish that saw fans furious at the SEC officials.

With 3:28 left in the game and down by three, Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell fired a second-down pass towards Rico Scott in the end zone.

But Georgia defensive back KJ Bolden didn't play the ball and made contact with Scott without turning his head to the backfield.

Those watching all waited for a flag to be thrown but officials determined it was not pass interference. The next play, Russell was sacked to move them out of field goal range, then Alabama punted and never got the ball back.

Head coach Kaleb DeBoer raged on the sidelines as officials decided not to throw a flag, while ESPN/ABC rules analyst Matt Austin saw a new angle as the Bulldogs kneeled out the clock to end the game.
news.summary: One week after being forced to back out of attending the SEC showdown between Georgia and Alabama, the President has reportedly canceled a trip to an NFL game this weekend.

news.title: Tension erupts during House midterm debate as Lawler fact-checks NY Democrat opponent on immigration
news.text:
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat opponent Cait Conley Wednesday night in a one-hour debate filled with interruptions and fiery accusations less than three weeks before Election Day.

Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York’s 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump’s term.

Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district.

Their most heated clashes came on the immigration front, when the moderator referenced the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last week in New York City while the man’s 5-year-old child was in the car.

DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY

The race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat veteran Cait Conley could decide the fate of the House of Representatives for the next two years. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

“I believe that border security is national security and that we do need immigration enforcement to ensure that violent criminals and drug cartels and human traffickers and terrorist organizations aren’t in our communities and that they are deported,” Conley said. 

“But what we are seeing right now with the conduct of ICE is posing a public safety hazard. To your point, last week, they shot into a car where there was a 5-year-old child. I’ll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you’re not permitted to do that kind of stuff.”

NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING

Lawler, however, pointed out the man has a lengthy criminal rap sheet and was seen by some as a danger to his community. He also argued the shooting would never have happened had local law enforcement not been barred from handing him over to ICE by New York’s sanctuary laws.

He said Conley “supports making New York a sanctuary state, prohibits cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials.”

WATCH: LAWLER UNLOADS ON RASKIN AFTER FIERY IMMIGRATION HEARING: ‘GROW THE F— UP’

Lawler later pivoted the discussion to Sheridan Gorman, the college student from his district who was killed while out with her friends near her campus in Chicago earlier this year. The illegal immigrant accused of killing her was previously charged with shoplifting, but Chicago sanctuary laws prevent local law enforcement from handing him over to ICE.

Police tape cordons off a street in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx after a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents last week. (WCBS)

Conley called Gorman’s death “an atrocious crime” while repeatedly pointing out it took place in Chicago.

Lawler attempted to intervene multiple times to call it “preventable,” to which an irate Conley responded, “Can I finish?”

“And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent citizens,” she said.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO ‘WITHHOLD FUNDING’ FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Lawler then argued, however, that Conley’s support of sanctuary policies runs counter to that.

“If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE, and he will be released under cashless bail,” Lawler said.

It prompted the moderator to step in, telling Lawler there was no “cross-examination round.”

Elsewhere in the debate, Lawler accused Conley of having “literally just lied” that Lawler voted with Trump “100% of the time.”

10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY

“I’ve been rated the third most independent member of my conference. And I have taken on the president on numerous issues, including lifting the cap on SALT, including extending Haitian TPS, including passing an extension for the ACA enhanced premium tax credit despite his objections,” Lawler said.

Earlier in the debate, Conley tried to accuse Lawler of supporting tax breaks for companies that build data centers as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Sheridan Gorman and her father, Tom Gorman, in a family photo. (Gorman Family/Fox News)

Lawler shot back, “I know you just moved here from Virginia, so it’s hard for you to understand the local communities, but the fact is … the provision you referenced in the Working Families Tax Cut Act is $80 billion for 100% expensing for every business in America to expense plant, property and equipment. 

“Are you against our small businesses in the Hudson Valley being able to expense their plant, property and equipment and hire more people? Your attack on that rings hollow. You clearly don’t understand what’s actually in the tax bill. And part of the problem is you don’t pay property taxes.”

Both candidates shook hands after their spirited debate and thanked each other for appearing. Lawler also thanked Conley for her military service.

The district is a pivotal one for control of the House next year. Lawler is one of three House Republicans who won a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris also won in 2024. 

And in an election that’s expected to be brutal for the GOP, both sides are pouring millions of dollars into the fight.

news.title: Democratic Icon, 80, to Boost Bid to Flip Deep Red State
news.text:
The Democratic Party is sending a veteran to the front lines.

Former President Bill Clinton, 80, will join Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly at an evening interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, next week, according to MS NOW.

Jolly, a former Republican congressman, easily won the Democratic nomination in April and is facing a heated matchup against Republican Rep. Byron Donalds to succeed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Clinton is making his first public campaign appearance only two weeks before the midterm elections, similar to how he campaigned in 2022. In the days leading up to the 2022 midterms, Clinton rallied Democrats in New York, New Jersey, and South Texas.

However, the 42nd POTUS was much busier in 2024, making dozens of appearances to support then-Vice President Kamala Harris and campaigning for multiple down-ballot Democrats.

Earlier this week, he appeared alongside Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries at a fundraiser in New York to support Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz. The Florida congressman is running in a newly remapped district after DeSantis signed a new congressional map into law in May.

Similar to President Donald Trump, Clinton has faced scrutiny over his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In February, he was brought in for a closed-door deposition by the House Oversight Committee as part of a probe into the Epstein files, which included photos of the former president alongside Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and numerous unidentified women.

Clinton insisted he did nothing wrong and had “no idea” about any of the crimes Epstein committed. He added that he saw nothing that “ever gave me pause.”

“As someone who grew up in a home with domestic abuse, not only would I not have flown on his plane if I had any inkling of what he was doing—I would have turned him in myself and led the call for justice for his crimes, not sweetheart deals,” he said in a statement shared on X at the time.

Government-released documents revealed Clinton traveled on Epstein’s private jet, nicknamed the Lolita Express, 16 times.

However, even Trump, 80, felt sympathy for his Democratic adversary.

“I don’t like seeing him deposed,” Trump said of Clinton at the time. “But they certainly went after me a lot more than that.”

Trump did not extend the same sympathy to Clinton’s wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who was also deposed the day before her husband.

news.title: Canadian singer Joni Mitchell officially becomes American citizen after 62-year journey
news.text: Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen at age 82, more than six decades after she first moved to the United States. The music icon, who hails from Canada, announced the news on Instagram, sharing a photo of herself beaming while holding an American flag along with a video from her naturalization ceremony. "A journey that began 62 years ago," Mitchell wrote in the caption of her post. ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY Mitchell wore a red and navy blue floral cardigan that had an American flag pin along with a red beaded necklace, a red beret and black pants with black boots while posing in between an American flag and a Department of Homeland Security flag. In the video Mitchell uploaded, she was seated in the front row at the ceremony as the speaker announced, "And Joni Mitchell, Canada" to cheers and applause from the audience. According to KSL, Mitchell will also retain her Canadian citizenship because the U.S. and Canada legally permit dual citizenship. The legendary singer-songwriter was born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, to Royal Canadian Air Force flight Lt. William Andrew Anderson and teacher Myrtle Marguerite. Mitchell's family lived on several bases during World War II before eventually settling in Saskatoon, which the singer has often referred to as her hometown. She went on to attend the Alberta College of Art in Calgary before dropping out and relocating to Toronto, where she played gigs at coffee houses and folk clubs. The "Both Sides Now" songstress moved to the United States in 1965 at age 21 after marrying American folk singer Chuck Mitchell. The former couple, who lived in Detroit, Michigan, performed together as a folk duo before divorcing in 1967. After their divorce, Mitchell left Detroit and moved to New York City, where she became part of the Greenwich Village folk scene and performed along the East Coast. By 1968, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, settling in Laurel Canyon, which was becoming a hub for singer-songwriters including David Crosby, Graham Nash and others. In the mid-1970s, Mitchell moved to LA's Bel Air neighborhood, where she lived in a historic 1920s home for decades. Mitchell built her legendary music career while living in California, where she recorded many of her most acclaimed albums, including "Blue," "Court and Spark" and "Ladies of the Canyon." Mitchell has won 11 Grammy Awards and was inducted into both the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1997. She was also recognized with the Kennedy Center Honors in 2021 and received the prestigious Library of Congress Gershwin Prize for Popular Song in 2023. The musician lives in Santa Barbara, California. Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and expressed frustration that she couldn't vote in U.S. elections because she was Canadian. CHRIS ROBINSON, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN FACE BACKLASH AS 'AMERICANS HAVE HAD ENOUGH' OF BEING LECTURED: EXPERT During a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in LA in October 2024, Mitchell slammed Trump while performing her 1985 song "Dog Eat Dog," according to Billboard. After singing a lyric about wealthy financiers, she added, "Like Donald Trump!" Following her performance of the song, Mitchell responded to an audience member who shouted an anti-Trump remark. "'F--- Donald Trump.' I love that song," she said, apparently referencing rapper YG's 2016 protest song "FDT (F--- Donald Trump)" featuring the late rapper and activist Nipsey Hussle. She then encouraged Americans to participate in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, in which Trump ran against Democratic nominee former Vice President Kamala Harris. "Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote . I'm Canadian. I'm one of those lousy immigrants," Mitchell said. Months before becoming an American citizen, Mitchell criticized the political climate in the U.S. while accepting a lifetime achievement award at Canada's Juno Awards in March. At the ceremony, Mitchell praised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, saying, "I'm so glad to be back in Canada. This man is a blessing. You guys are so fortunate." After Mitchell's comments at the Juno Awards, the White House issued a dismissive response. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? news.title: Democrats Turn to Bill Clinton for Late Campaign Push in Florida
news.text:
Former President Bill Clinton is joining Florida Democrats’ late push for votes, with a campaign appearance for gubernatorial nominee David Jolly scheduled two weeks before Election Day.

Clinton will appear alongside Jolly at an evening interfaith event in Hollywood on Tuesday, October 20. The visit will mark his first public campaign stop of the 2026 midterms, according to Jolly’s campaign.

The former president’s appearance comes as Jolly, a former Republican congressman who won the Democrat nomination in August, faces Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Democrats are bringing Clinton into a state where they have struggled for decades to win the governor’s office. Lawton Chiles was the last Democrat elected governor of Florida, winning reelection in 1994. Jolly is seeking to break that streak on November 3, but recent surveys offer different pictures of his chances against Donalds.

Clinton’s visit comes after a Stetson University poll released Tuesday showed Donalds ahead of Jolly by 11 points, 52% to 41%, among modeled likely voters. Other polling has shown a narrower contest. A St. Pete Polls survey conducted October 5–7 put the candidates at 45% each, while a YouGov survey released last week showed Donalds ahead 47% to 45%.

Clinton’s visit will take place as early voting begins in parts of Florida, giving Jolly a prominent Democrat surrogate during the final stretch of the campaign. The governor’s race is also drawing attention beyond the state.

The Cook Political Report moved the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” earlier this month, keeping Republicans favored while acknowledging a more competitive race. The change came despite Donalds’ substantial financial advantage over Jolly. Clinton’s help for Florida Democrats extends beyond the governor’s contest.

Clinton and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries headlined a New York fundraiser earlier this week for Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-FL), MS NOW reported. Moskowitz is seeking reelection in a newly drawn district described by the outlet as a toss-up after a DeSantis-backed congressional remapping altered his previous seat.

The former president has made similar late appearances in previous elections. During the 2022 midterms, he campaigned in New York, New Jersey, and South Texas in the closing days before voters went to the polls.

He took on a larger role in 2024, making dozens of campaign stops across battleground states for then-Vice President Kamala Harris while also supporting candidates further down the ballot.

news.title: Kimberly Who?
news.text:
Four years later, Guilfoyle had become less helper than headache. Trump, Jr., had been seen with another woman, a Palm Beach socialite to whom he is now married, and the couple’s engagement was called off. “I had to get her out of here,” Trump reportedly told people. (The White House has denied that Trump made this statement.) The solution: naming Guilfoyle Ambassador to Greece, a country with which she had no clear ties—her mother is from Puerto Rico, her father from Ireland—but that became, or so it appeared, a convenient place to stash the inconvenient ex.
Those who had paid attention to Guilfoyle’s past might have questioned her diplomatic skills. She was forced to leave Fox in 2018 over allegations of questionable workplace behavior. Two years later, my colleague Jane Mayer reported on the details: one of Guilfoyle’s assistants had accused her of repeated sexual harassment. The assistant, Mayer wrote, claimed to have been subject to “degrading, abusive, and sexually inappropriate behavior; among other things, she said that she was frequently required to work at Guilfoyle’s New York apartment while the Fox host displayed herself naked, and was shown photographs of the genitalia of men with whom Guilfoyle had had sexual relations.” (Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing.) Fox paid “upward of four million dollars” to settle the complaint.
On Tuesday, Guilfoyle was forced to resign from the ambassadorship a year into the post, for problems of a different nature: financial, not sexual, although her provocative attire as Ambassador also drew attention. (Among other fashion choices, Guilfoyle, who travels with a stylist, wore a see-through black lace dress to a Thanksgiving dinner hosted by the American-Hellenic Chamber of Commerce.) The Wall Street Journal had published a devastating trio of stories about Guilfoyle’s behavior on the job. First came a piece in late September about Guilfoyle’s unusually dogged advocacy on behalf of a Greek construction firm, the Aktor Group, which was seeking to break into the energy business; Christos Marafatsos, a top lobbyist for the company, “has attended so many of her meetings that some foreign officials mistook him for her chief of staff,” the Journal wrote. (Aktor and attorneys for Guilfoyle have denied any improprieties.) Then, last week, the Journal reported on Guilfoyle’s beseeching a Trump donor to wire her a hundred thousand dollars to pay her American Express bill in advance of her confirmation hearing. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” Guilfoyle texted the donor, Eric Deters, adding a prayer-hands emoji. Deters, a Kentucky lawyer and former congressional candidate, had already paid Guilfoyle three hundred thousand dollars; among other things he sought a meeting with the commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service to discuss his tax problems. “As of this memo, I have not received one favor,” Deters wrote. “I am not naive or a sucker. I need results.”
Guilfoyle, a lawyer and former prosecutor—she overlapped with Kamala Harris in the San Francisco district attorney’s office—understood the risk posed by Deters’s digital trail. “Stop papering all these things,” she warned, advising Deters to call her on Signal instead. “It’s really dangerous.” Deters ultimately balked at the AmEx payment. “I can’t do this without getting a divorce,” he told Guilfoyle. (Guilfoyle has suggested the texts were generated by A.I. and said, “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”)
The Journal’s final blow, on Saturday, described how Guilfoyle accepted luxury travel, including from a Greek shipping magnate who hosted Guilfoyle on his private jet and paid her bill at the Four Seasons Hotel George V, in Paris, while she was in town to attend his wife’s fashion show. Lobbying an unnamed U.S. businessman to secure an invitation to a dinner at the World Economic Forum in Davos in honor of Eric Trump, Guilfoyle promised, “I’m going to make you a lot of fucking money,” according to a recording reviewed by the Journal.
The paradox of Trump Administration corruption is that the most egregious offenders—the President chief among them—operate in plain sight and on a grand scale. They don’t fret, to borrow Guilfoyle’s verb, about “papering” the evidence; they consider themselves, perhaps with good reason, immune from consequences. To borrow from Nixon’s answer to David Frost, when the President does it, that means it is not grifting. Trump imposed some constraints on his own and his immediate family’s dealings during his first term—he promised, for example, that the Trump Organization would not conduct business abroad—but these limits, such as they were, have been shrugged off in the second. As Trump explained to the Times in January, “I found out that nobody cared. . . . I got absolutely no credit for it.”
My colleague David Kirkpatrick calculated that during the first year of his second term, Trump and his family leveraged the Presidency to make more than four billion dollars, dealing in cryptocurrency, foreign real-estate investments, and prediction markets. That total does not include the potential value of Trump’s collusive “settlement” of a private lawsuit against the I.R.S. for the leak of his tax information; as part of the arrangement, the government agreed that Trump, his family, and his companies would be immune from back taxes and penalties. Meanwhile, the President’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is both an unpaid negotiator for the Trump Administration and the owner of an investment firm, Affinity Partners, that is almost entirely financed by Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries.
When there are consequences for Trump family members’ overreach, they tend toward the minimum. Last month, ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin had paid hundreds of thousands in expenses for Donald Trump, Jr., and his new wife, Bettina Anderson Trump’s May wedding celebration, including renting out a private island and putting on a fireworks display. The President described this arrangement as “very common” and “totally allowed,” but said his son was repaying the oligarch. Contrast that seeming nonchalance with Trump’s response to reports of profiteering by James Blair and Chris LaCivita, two of his senior political advisers. On October 6th, the Times reported that, in the heat of the U.S. midterm campaign, the pair had travelled to Republika Srpska, a self-governing territory in the Balkans, to help the pro-Russia government in advance of its own elections. Blair, the former deputy White House chief of staff, and LaCivita, a co-manager of Trump’s 2024 campaign, were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars through a Washington law firm, the Times said. Trump, typically, diminished his relationship with the two men, calling them “outside consultants” who “do not work for me.” He added, “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”
Guilfoyle would seem to require particularly careful handling. Having dated Don, Jr., for years, she presumably knows a lot of Trump family and Trump business secrets. So it was something of a surprise that the White House opted not to accord her the ordinary face-saving courtesy of announcing her own departure. Instead, the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, said Guilfoyle had been asked to resign. Zacharia added, incongruously, “She has been a wonderful asset to the team.” What, one wonders, would count as a liability? ♦
news.summary: In this Administration, former Ambassador Guilfoyle is the rare Trump associate to face consequences for misdeeds.

news.title: Republicans Get New Midterm Warning Sign as Kansas Senate Race Shifts
news.text: Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball has shifted numerous U.S. Senate races in favor of Democrats on Wednesday, including Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall's seat in Kansas versus Democrat Adam Hamilton. The forecaster has moved the race from Leans Republican to a Toss-Up. Marshall, a doctor, is currently in the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party. In a post on Truth Social discussing a potential rally for Marshall in the near future, President Donald Trump called him one of his "favorite Senators." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Hamilton campaign spokesperson Glynnis Harvey told Newsweek when asked about the new shift from Sabato’s Crystal Ball, "Roger Marshall abandoned Kansas. Instead of fighting for Kansas farmers, aviation workers, and families, he’s been a yes-man to corruption in Washington, supporting policies that are driving up costs and cutting healthcare. Republicans, Democrats, and Independents across Kansas are connecting with Adam’s message of leading from the middle to lower costs and solve our nation’s biggest problems. Kansans are ready for change.” Newsweek reached out to Marshall's campaign via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know Sabato’s Crystal Ball said they were initially hesitant to move the race into the Toss-Up category, "but a full-on Republican rescue operation appears underway for Marshall," which helped in part move the needle, the forecaster said. The election forecaster also pointed to the Senate Leadership Fund investing heavily in the race, citing Punchbowl News. "We noted last week that, for the first time all cycle, Republicans now needed to win more Toss-ups than Democrats did in order to win the Senate, and the Kansas move—a GOP-held state—now means Republicans need 4 of the 5 Toss-ups to hold the Senate, while Democrats still just need two," the forecaster said in part. The U.S. Senate races that shifted in the new update, besides Kansas, are Nebraska from Likely Republican to Leans Republican, New Hampshire from Leans Democratic to Likely Democratic, Minnesota from Likely Democratic to Leans Democratic and Mississippi from Safe Republican to Likely Republican. The Cook Political Report currently has the race rated as a Toss-Up as well, adding to the potentially troubling signs for Republicans surrounding the contest. Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Wednesday, "Moving Kansas from Lean Republican to Toss-up is a real warning for Republicans, not a full red alert. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, so any serious threat there means the national environment is biting harder than expected. Senate Leadership Fund already dropped millions into Marshall’s race. That is the tell." Agranoff continued: "When the party has to spend heavily to hold a seat that should be safe, it pulls resources from other fights. Hamilton is not a household name, and Marshall still has the structural edge. A toss-up rating in a deep red state is what forces campaigns to treat it like a real contest instead of a formality. It is not the race that decides the majority by itself, but it is the kind of race that makes holding the majority harder." In his post earlier this week, Trump praised Marshall, calling him a wonderful person who has been given a "bum rap" for allegedly requesting money owed to him by his patients. Marshall had branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." Trump also threw jabs at Hamilton, saying that he loves high taxes, open borders and added that he wouldn't want the Democrat to be his pastor. The president accused Hamilton of mishandling allegations involving a church camp counselor whom Trump called a child predator. Hamilton's campaign has previously rejected those attacks and also told the Kansas Reflector in July that "there was no attempt at a cover-up" regarding the investigation into the counselor following reports of abuse beginning in 2005, the outlet says. “I can just say that our aim was to make sure that if we got anything wrong, we wanted to get it right,” Hamilton said to the outlet. Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area congregation in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. What Recent Polling Shows Recent polling shows Hamilton in the lead by a couple of points or a dead heat. Prediction market site Polymarket shows Marshall ahead with 63 percent versus Hamilton's 38 percent on Wednesday afternoon. A YouGov poll showed Hamilton with 48 percent of the potential vote compared to Marshall's 45 percent. One percent said someone else, 5 percent said undecided and 1 percent said they would not vote. The poll surveyed 2,255 likely voters in Kansas from September 24 to October 4 and had a 3.2 percent margin of error. An InsiderAdvantage poll shows Hamilton with 47.5 percent of the vote compared to Marshall's 46.7 percent. Libertarian Party candidate David C. Graham landed 3.4 percent of the vote, and 2.4 percent were undecided. The poll was conducted from October 9-10, 2026, among 1,200 likely voters and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. A Trafalgar Group poll showed Hamilton had 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Graham and 10.1 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and had a margin of error of 2.9 percent. news.title: Josh Turek Is Winning Over Iowa Trump Voters, Poll Finds
news.text: A new poll shows that Democrat Josh Turek is winning over people who voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election in the race to be Iowa's next U.S. senator. The Hawkeye State is among this year's most competitive Senate races, as Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson vie for the open seat left by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Polls continue pointing to a tight race between the two candidates after their first debate last week, where tariffs, immigration and voting records played a major role. Both candidates have also exchanged verbal blows regarding the state's economy and the best path forward as Iowans express concerns about inflation and surging fuel costs. The new poll from YouGov comes after Turek and Hinson faced off in a second debate on Tuesday night. Josh Turek vs. Ashley Hinson: What Latest Polls Show After Debate In the YouGov poll, which surveyed 2,245 likely Iowa voters from October 6 to October 12, Turek led Hinson 47 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent of voters still undecided. And not only did Turek lead in the most recent poll between the two candidates, it also appears he is winning over Iowans who previously voted for Trump. According to the poll, 41 percent of respondents backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, compared with 52 percent who voted for Trump. Given Turek's current edge, the results suggest he has won support from at least some voters who previously cast ballots for Trump. The margin of error was 3.1 percent. Turek's lead over Hinson is narrower in the YouGov poll than in other recent surveys. A poll by Suffolk University conducted from October 1 to October 4 gave him a 4-point lead over Hinson, 48 percent to 44 percent. Turek had a 2-point lead over Hinson in several other recent polls, including a Beacon Research analysis from September 24 to September 28 that favored him over Hinson at 49 percent to 47 percent. An InsiderAdvantage poll held on September 22 and September 23 gave Turek a 1-point lead over Hinson at 47 percent to 46 percent, whereas a Marist University poll taken from September 17 to September 20 gave Turek a heftier 8-point lead over Hinson, 50 percent to 42 percent. Several polls have also shown Hinson ahead. A recent one by Emerson College on October 5 and October 6 favored Hinson for the race at 47 percent to Turek's 45 percent. A CNN poll conducted from September 29 to October 5 also gave Hinson a 2-point lead, at 45 percent to Turek's 43 percent. Hinson carried the same 2-point leads over Turek in two Quantus Insights polls on September 28 and September 29, and a 1-point lead in a New York Times/Siena University poll taken from September 22 to October 1. Newsweek reached out to the campaigns for Turek and Hinson by email on Wednesday. Since the second debate between the two candidates was held on Tuesday night, it did not influence the outcome of the YouGov poll. The poll also allowed some insight into Trump's approval in Iowa, with the majority disapproving of the president's performance. When asked if they approved of Trump's work as president so far, 29 percent said they strongly approved, while 17 percent said somewhat approved. Five percent said they somewhat disapproved, while 49 percent said they strongly disapproved. One percent said they were unsure. What Prediction Markets Show Prediction markets show a less tight race. Both Polymarket and Kalshi show Hinson with a generous lead over Turek. On Polymarket, Hinson is favored to win the Senate race at 57 percent to Turek's 42 percent. She has a slightly greater lead on Kalshi, where she is favored to win at 58 percent to Turek's 42 percent. Why the Iowa Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms This year's midterm elections could flip control of the House and Senate as Republican candidates work to overcome widespread American concerns tied to the economy, inflation, rising fuel costs and the Iran war. Although Iowa has voted Republican in the Senate elections since 2008, the state has also had a history of voting for presidential candidates from both political parties, making the current political environment a competitive one. Trump won Iowa the last three election cycles, but before that, former President Barack Obama won the state twice. The recent poll delivered encouraging news for Turek's campaign, considering the last time Democrats won an Iowa Senate election was 18 years ago, when incumbent Senator Tom Harkin defeated his Republican opponent, Christopher Reed. In the elections since, Ernst and Republican Chuck Grassley have held control of Iowa's two Senate seats. What Happens Next Early voting in Iowa began Tuesday and will continue through November 2. The midterm elections take place on November 3. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: A new poll shows that Democrat Josh Turek is winning over people who voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

news.title: AOC, JD Vance Head to Michigan as Polls Show Tight El-Sayed-Rogers Race
news.text: New York Democrat Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Vice President JD Vance will make competing appearances in Michigan on Thursday as they campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Republican rival Mike Rogers, respectively, injecting national political star power and potential 2028 presidential intrigue into one of the country's most closely watched races. Vance is scheduled to headline a Trump 47 Committee rally in Monroe, Michigan, while Ocasio-Cortez will join El-Sayed for events in Iron Mountain and Marquette. In a statement announcing the campaign swing, Ocasio-Cortez said El-Sayed had "built a winning coalition with an agenda to bring down costs for Michigan families" and said she was excited to join him during the final stretch of the race. El-Sayed welcomed the endorsement, calling Ocasio-Cortez a "critical partner" during the primary and saying he looked forward to campaigning with her in the closing weeks. Vance's appearance comes as Republicans seek to shore up support in one of the country's most closely watched Senate races. During an earlier Michigan visit alongside Rogers, Republican National Committee spokesman Hunter Lovell said that "President Trump and Vice President JD Vance are leading the charge to elect a powerhouse Republican ticket in Michigan." Newsweek contacted the campaigns of El-Sayed and Rogers for comment. Why Michigan Matters Michigan, a perennial presidential battleground, is expected to be one of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds in the country, helping determine which party controls the chamber after the midterm. The dueling appearances by Ocasio-Cortez and Vance give Michigan voters a rare chance to compare two of the most prominent younger voices in their respective parties. The events could offer clues about which political messages resonate in a state that has repeatedly played a decisive role in national elections. Democratic strategist Joel Payne told The Hill that Michigan's Senate race could have implications well beyond November. "The one race in 2026 that will impact what happens in 2028 is the Michigan Senate race," he said, adding that the contest "will set the tone for the 2028 primary field." A July Michigan poll found Ocasio-Cortez polling third among prospective 2028 Democratic presidential contenders, behind only former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Senator Jon Ossoff, while finishing ahead of California Governor Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. More than 20 percent of respondents were undecided. What the Latest El-Sayed-Rogers Polls Show Six polls conducted in late September and early October have given El-Sayed a lead from between 1 and 7 percentage points. The newest, an InsiderAdvantage survey of 1,200 likely voters conducted October 9-10, put El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent, with 5 percent undecided. Wedgewood Polls was in the field the two days prior and put El-Sayed at 53 percent to Rogers' 47 percent among 607 likely voters. Other recent surveys showed a race inside the margin of error. Quantus Insights found El-Sayed up 48 percent to 47 percent among 744 likely voters polled October 5-6. YouGov, working with a much larger sample of 3,947 likely voters September 22-October 4, also landed on a one-point gap, 49 percent to 48 percent. news.title: CNN: Mamdani, Hochul Drag Down New York Democrats
news.text:
CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said Wednesday that Republicans are polling at historically strong levels among Jewish voters in New York, citing surveys that show Democrat margins with the group falling by more than 35 points since 2022.

Enten, appearing alongside co-anchor John Berman, said no state has a larger Jewish share of the electorate than New York, and that recent polling showed the group moving toward the GOP in both the governor’s race and the contest for the U.S. House, figures he also posted on X.

The data analyst traced the governor’s race first, putting the current Democrat margin among Jewish voters at 13 points. That is down from the 51-point lead Gov. Kathy Hochul held in 2022 and Andrew Cuomo’s 55-point edge in 2018.

“We’re talking about a swing here … of 38 points downward towards the Republicans when it comes to Jewish voters,” Enten said.

The House generic ballot shows a similar move, he added, with the Democrat lead among Jewish voters narrowing from 49 points in 2022 to 13 points this year.

“Their lead is absolutely tumbled into the Hudson River among Jewish voters,” the CNN analyst said.

Asked by Berman about the mayor’s role, the analyst pointed to Democratic Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose positions on Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, he said, do not line up with many Jewish New Yorkers. Enten put Mamdani’s net favorability among Jewish voters at minus 23, roughly 31 points below his standing with the overall New York electorate.

A September Siena University poll tracked the same pattern. Among Jewish voters, Republican Bruce Blakeman led Hochul 46% to 43% in the governor’s race, even as Hochul led by nine points statewide. Jewish voters also preferred Blakeman over Hochul on addressing “undocumented immigrants,”48% to 43%, and viewed Mamdani unfavorably, 64% to 33%.

The polling follows Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor in November, when exit polls showed him taking about a third of the city’s Jewish vote while Cuomo, running as an independent, carried roughly 63%.

Enten closed on New York’s 17th Congressional District, held by Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY) in a seat Kamala Harris carried in 2024 by less than a percentage point. The prediction market Kalshi gave Lawler a 39% chance of holding the heavily Jewish district, Enten noted, a figure he said could climb if Jewish voters break the way the polling suggests.

“They may just save Mike Lawler’s seat in Congress for him,” Enten said.

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said Wednesday that Republicans are polling at historically strong levels among Jewish voters in New York, citing surveys that show Democrat margins with the group falling by more than 35 points since 2022.

news.title: Joe Biden faces the ultimate humiliation as his presidential library dream hits the rocks... and an old friend refuses to donate to his 'tarnished legacy'
news.text:
Perhaps the worst legacy for a president is to be forgotten – and that increasingly appears to be the unfortunate fate awaiting Joe Biden.

In June, Barack Obama's $850 million museum opened to wild fanfare in Chicago, while Donald Trump's $1 billion future presidential library, a gleaming edifice draped in gold, is expected to tower over Miami.

Meanwhile, Biden now potentially faces the ignominy of having no new building at all.

'No real library will ever be built,' one major Democratic donor told the Daily Mail. 'Sadly, for him, that ship has sailed.'

Shunned by donors, lambasted for what they see as his selfishness and failure, Biden has become a former president not even Democrats want to remember.

The records from his administration are currently held by the National Archives, administered from room 1501 on the first floor of a government facility in Maryland. Where they will end up is anyone's guess.

According to the latest tax records filed by the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation, for the financial year 2024, it had $4 million in funding, all of which was left over from the failed 2024 campaign.

The foundation had spent just $21,348 on equipment, according to the filing. Another tax form suggested it hopes to raise $11.3 million, a pittance compared to Obama and Trump. Its 2025 tax return was due by May 15, 2026, but has not been filed. Tax-exempt organizations are allowed to receive an automatic six-month extension. 

'I can't speak for other donors, only myself, but I will not be contributing to it,' John Morgan, a top Democratic donor, told the Daily Mail in a statement.

'While I still have deep respect for the man I once knew, his legacy was tarnished by the decisions of those closest to him.'

That is a sentiment held by many who feel Biden was let down by advisers who pushed him to seek reelection in 2024, despite concerns about his age.

It led to the debacle of the first presidential debate against Donald Trump, in which Biden delivered a catastrophic performance.

Initial intentions for Biden's library were said to have involved hopes of raising several hundred million dollars to create an 'immersive museum.'

In September last year, the former president announced the library would be in his home state of Delaware but there has still been no confirmation of a site.

According to records released by the Mayor of Wilmington's office to Spotlight Delaware under freedom of information laws, officials from the city have been working with Biden representatives. The mayor's office declined to also release them to the Daily Mail on the grounds that the application was not from a Delaware citizen. 

The records showed that, in March last year, a Biden official emailed the mayor's office to say his team was 'working to get the lay of the land regarding potential sites in Wilmington' and they wanted to know more about plans for economic development.

The Biden team was particularly interested in an area called Riverfront East along the Christina River and asked for a 'deep dive' into it.

Two weeks later there was a meeting in Wilmington between city and Biden officials.

A 38-page presentation produced by the city showed how Riverfront East had been transformed by the state-funded Riverfront Development Corporation using financial incentives to stimulate private investment.

It said zoning laws would allow for a maximum six-story building.

The plan also said there was 'an availability of construction funding,' with $48 million of $60 million allocated to the area by the state of Delaware spent so far.

The Mayor of Wilmington's office did not respond to a request from the Daily Mail on whether that meant state taxpayer money could be used toward any library project.

The Presidential Libraries Act of 1955 bans federal funds, but not state ones, being used to build presidential libraries.

Also detailed in the presentation was an area in downtown Wilmington near the former headquarters of MBNA, the financial services company

Biden was once dubbed the 'Senator for MBNA' because it was his biggest donor during his time in the Senate, and also hired his son Hunter when he was in his 20s.

A separate cost-effective option for the eventual home of Biden's presidential documents is his alma mater, the University of Delaware.

It already has his records from his time in the Senate and as Vice President, and in 2018 opened the Joseph R Biden, Jr School of Public Policy and Administration, raising the possibility of housing the presidential documents in an existing building.

In February, Biden joined members of the 13-strong board he has appointed to oversee the library project for a private dinner at Longwood Gardens in Pennsylvania.

The only record of the event appeared to be a brief Instagram post by his daughter Ashley.

'I am grateful to all who acknowledge, celebrate, and honor Dads lifetime of public service,' she wrote.

The office of the Joseph R Biden Jr. Presidential Library at the National Archives Records Administration in Maryland said it does not handle funding or construction issues.

'To date, President Biden has not indicated his intentions with regard to a Presidential Library,' a representative told the Daily Mail.

The Office of Joe and Jill Biden did not respond to a request for comment on how much has been raised, or whether a site has been chosen. 

Biden himself has been focused on his book Promise Me, America, which is due out after the midterms on November 17.

Donors remain irate at him for his decision to attempt to run for a second term in his 80s, which ultimately led to Kamala Harris taking over and being defeated by Donald Trump.

Amid lingering frustration, insiders say money that could have gone to Biden's library project is being directed instead to Democratic campaigns in the midterms.

One official who worked with Biden in the White House previously told the Daily Mail he was 'selfish,' had found the presidency 'intoxicating,' and surrounded himself with advisers who were not 'willing to speak truth to power.'

'They did the country a disservice, but ultimately, the buck stops with him, and he bears the responsibility for what was a very reckless decision,' they said.

The Presidential Library system began in 1939 when President Franklin D Roosevelt gave his records to the government and donors raised money for a library.

Since then, all presidents have taken similar measures to preserve their legacy, with some magnificent buildings created in the process.

The privately funded cost for the buildings has soared exponentially, even before Obama and Trump.

In 1997, the George HW Bush library cost $43 million. Bill Clinton’s was $165 million, and George W Bush’s $500 million.

Delaware Governor Matt Meyer has previously welcomed Biden's decision to base his library there.

Meyer said: 'To Delaware, he will always be our favorite. The new presidential library here in Delaware will give future generations the chance to see his story of resilience, family and never forgetting your roots.
news.summary: In June, Barack Obama's $850 million museum opened to wild fanfare in Chicago, while Donald Trump's $1 billion future presidential library is expected to tower over Miami.

news.title: Who Could Replace Donald Trump in 2028? Inside Americans' Top Picks for the Next Presidential Election
news.text:
A new poll is offering an early look at who Americans want to see replace President Trump on the ballot in 2028.

The latest Focaldata-Financial Times survey, released October 11, 2026, asked 2,553 U.S. adults about the next presidential election. The poll also measured Trump’s current job performance and top voter concerns.

The results show a clear frontrunner on each side of the aisle, with Vice President JD Vance leading Republicans and former Vice President Kamala Harris leading Democrats.Kamala Harris Leads Democrats as Top Choice for 2028When it comes to the Democratic primary, Harris is the early favorite.

According to the poll, 32% of respondents asked about the Democratic field selected Harris as their first choice for 2028.

The remaining spots are taken by California Governor Gavin Newsom, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

The data shows a sharp age divide for Harris. She received 49% support among respondents aged 18-29 and 37% among those aged 30-39.

Her support drops among older voters, as a portion of those aged 70 and older selected her, compared to 23% in that age group who chose Newsom.JD Vance Dominates Republican Field With Wide LeadOn the Republican side, Vance holds a commanding early lead. 

The poll found that 38% of respondents asked about the Republican primary selected Vance as their first choice.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio follows with 20%, while Florida Governor Ron DeSantis received 9% and Donald Trump Jr. received 8%. Another 13% said they were unsure.

Unlike Harris, Vance’s support was relatively consistent across age groups, showing broad appeal across generations.

Rubio did best with older voters. He got 31% from those who were 70 and older, but just 12% from the group of 18-29.Inflation Remains Top Concern for VotersThe poll also asked Americans about the issues that matter most to them heading toward 2028.

Inflation and the cost of living remain the top concerns, with 54% of respondents citing them as major issues. Jobs and the economy followed, along with health care as other major concerns.

The survey comes as voters continue to weigh the current administration’s handling of economic issues ahead of the next election cycle.What Americans Think of Trump’s Job PerformanceThe Focaldata-Financial Times poll also measured how Americans feel about Trump's job performance.

According to the survey, just 13% said they strongly approve of the job Trump is doing, while another 20% said they somewhat approve.

The poll provides one of the earliest snapshots of voter sentiment more than two years out from the presidential election. Both parties are showing clear early frontrunners, but with a significant portion of voters still undecided.
news.summary: A new survery by Focaldata-Financial Times on October 11, 2026, revealed the candidates who are expected to replace Donald Trump in 2028.

news.title: Kamala Harris adds stops to her final midterm campaign stretch. Her decision about 2028 comes later
news.text:
By BILL BARROW

ATLANTA (AP) — Kamala Harris is building out her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats, completing a midterm schedule that by Election Day will have taken her to multiple early presidential primary states on Democrats’ 2028 calendar as the former vice president mulls whether to seek the White House again.

Spanning from Oct. 21 to Oct. 30, Harris’ expanded closing stretch will now include New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Mississippi, along with a Florida virtual event, according to a schedule her office shared first with The Associated Press. Harris already had announced late October stops in Georgia and Nevada.

Harris has said in multiple recent interviews that she’s focused on helping Democrats win in November. But she has not ruled out another presidential campaign after losing the 2024 general election to Donald Trump.

“For the past twenty months, the American people have struggled as a consequence of the cruelty and corruption of this current administration,” Harris wrote in a fundraising email Wednesday to donors asking them to support her travels via her Fight for The People PAC. “Now is the time for us to be ruthless in delivering for the people: on affordability, on fighting corruption, and on making our voices heard.”

Her late October tour focuses on nominees for governor and U.S. Senate, including pairings that put the first Black woman to serve as vice president alongside potential history-making candidates.

Harris will open Oct. 21 in Nevada with Aaron Ford, the state’s first Black attorney general who would be the state’s first Black governor, and other candidates. She’ll also meet with Culinary Workers Union members. Nevada holds the second 2028 presidential nominating contest, after South Carolina.

On Oct. 22, she will be in Mississippi with Scott Colom, who would be the state’s first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom has recently begun to garner more attention from national Democrats as he faces Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

From Mississippi, Harris will head to New Hampshire on Oct. 24 to campaign with Senate nominee Chris Pappas and participate in a discussion on reproductive care and abortion rights. As vice president, Harris was the Biden White House’s foremost abortion rights advocate, especially during the 2022 midterm campaign. New Hampshire comes third in Democrats’ 2028 primary order.

Harris and Wisconsin gubernatorial nominee David Crowley will campaign together Oct. 26. Harris will finish with a three-day swing in Georgia that begins Oct. 28. She will campaign with Sen. Jon Ossoff, attend voter protection events and speak Oct. 30 at the Fulton County Democratic Party’s annual gala in Atlanta.

While in Georgia, Harris will headline a virtual organizing event with Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon, who would be her state’s first Black U.S. senator. That will put Harris, who hails from the Democrats’ liberal establishment, alongside one of the party’s most progressive nominees. A state lawmaker, Nixon identifies as a democratic socialist and draws support from many left-flank activists who in 2024 criticized Harris as too moderate.

The itinerary follows earlier in-person and online campaign appearances and fundraisers, along with voter protection and organizing events Harris helped lead, including for the Democratic National Committee. Most recently, Harris was in Michigan to campaign for Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed—another notable progressive Democratic nominee—and speak at an NAACP event.
news.summary: Kamala Harris is building out her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats, completing a midterm schedule that by Election Day will have taken her to multiple early presidential primary states on Democrats’ 2028 calendar as the former vice president mulls whether to seek the White House again.

news.title: Newsom heads to New Hampshire to stump for Democrats, raise political profile
news.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom is headed to New Hampshire this weekend to campaign for Democratic candidates in the November election, a continuation of his reconnaissance tour through swing states in preparation for a possible 2028 presidential run. The trip follows voyages to other early primary voting states, including South Carolina in September and Nevada in July, that could be critical to his campaign if he officially joins the race. “I think if your travel calendar aligns with the Democratic Party's primary calendar, you're probably running for president,” said Thad Kousser, a professor of political science at UC San Diego. It’s still too early for Newsom, or any other would-be presidential contender, to declare their candidacy, Kousser said, but the governor’s movements are typical of a politician who is “all in.” “This is the clearest signal to voters, to donors, and to the chattering class that you're willing to put in the hard yards, the years of on-the-ground campaigning, that it takes to do well in one of these primaries or caucuses,” he said. Newsom isn’t alone. A cadre of potential 2028 candidates, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, among others, is also deploying a similiar shadow campaign strategy and raising money for swing-state Democrats in the midterms. The governor’s visit to New Hampshire comes after he raised a half of a million dollars for New Hampshire Democrats this election cycle. His fundraising supported a new field office for the state party in Nashua, where he’ll join gubernatorial candidate Cinde Warmington and Rep. Chris Pappas, who is vying against a Republican for the U.S. Senate, at a canvassing event on Saturday morning. Newsom, Pappas and Warmington will appear at a second campaign event in Exeter together at 1 p.m. before Newsom heads to an early evening meet and greet with Stefany Shaheen, a House candidate, in Manchester. After returning from New Hampshire, Newsom plans to participate in campaign events across California in support of Democrats in newly redistricted congressional seats. The Harris campaign said she also plans to stump for Pappas in New Hampshire on Oct. 24. As she considers a third bid for the White House, Harris is visiting Nevada, Mississippi, Wisconsin and Georgia in the final days of the midterm election cycle. Kousser said Harris’ schedule suggests she wants to keep her options open. “These candidates are reaching out to the direct audience of voters, endorsers, and key leaders in those states, and they're also trying to show the national audience that they have a fire in the belly and that they're willing to put in the work,” he said. While Newsom mirrors the moves of a presidential candidate, his comments have fueled speculation about whether he will ultimately run. Newsom recently said that if Harris is in, he's out. The governor, who made similar statements in the past, said it would be "mutually-assured destruction" and there would be too much crossover between the two California political heavyweights, who would be vying for the same donors and supporters while offering a similar policy profile. The governor has also said the decision lies with his family and that his four children need to be "on board."
news.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's trip follows voyages to other early primary voting states that could be critical to his campaign if he officially joins the 2028 presidential contest.

news.title: Valkyries Star Gabby Williams Once Shared Jordan Brand Deal Perk That Keeps Her Wardrobe Fresh
news.text:
From wearing jeans banned back in the league’s early years to the high-fashion and streetwear influence seen in players’ “tunnel fits” now, the WNBA’s current era is a major indication of how times have changed. And just as she is making a name for herself on the court, Golden State Valkyries star Gabby Williams is part of this change. However, she has an added advantage that suits her wardrobe to the fullest, that being her endorsement deal with the Jordan brand.

Williams is widely known for wearing outfits with an elevated sporty look. And the Jordan brand happily accommodates her with an abundance of gear, something which she pointed out last year during her appearance on the Club 520 podcast. During that episode, the then Seattle Storm player was asked whether she receives ’20 pairs of shoes and 100 outfits’ in a truck that comes to her house. And that guess was actually correct.

“Honestly, yeah. Everything I have on now is the first time I have put it on. I feel like I don’t really gotta wear things twice, honestly.” Williams, who believes the Jordan brand represents her as a person, said on the Club 520 podcast last July.

“Jordan, compared to any other brand I have been with, they send us these elite packages every month. So you have what’s coming out, they always keep us looking nice. Jordan has made me some PEs, which I love. Sometimes I wear my PEs so much, I get sick of them. So I try to mix it up.” She added.

Apart from the gear, shoes are obviously what defines the Jordan brand. And while Williams does not have her own signature shoe line as of now, she has frequently worn exclusive player editions (PEs) and signature models such as the Jordan Heir Series 2 PE, Jordan Luka 5 “Graffiti”, and Jordan Triangle “NY vs. NY” during WNBA games.

The French star was one of Jordan Brand’s premier female endorsement signings in 2023. The announcement was made from a sleek pop-up design studio in Paris, France, and three of Jordan’s signature athletes, Luka Doncic, Jayson Tatum, and Zion Williamson, were present to welcome Williams.

“It just doesn’t even feel real, that they would do this announcement during QUAI 54 in France… Being a part of this has given me a lot of hope, just seeing Jordan’s engagement on the women’s side. I’ve been here and signed for a week [laughs], and already, they’ve taken an interest in things I want to do outside of just being a player.” Williams said upon signing with the Jordan Brand, via Boardroom.

And of course, Williams also took a moment to reflect on her favorite Michael Jordan moment now that she was affiliated with his brand.

“The Flu Game. Because there’s moments where I don’t feel good, and I’m like, ‘Ok, today is my MJ Flu Game — put me in!’ It’s my motivation.“ Williams said, while also revealing the Air Jordan 1 and the baby blue pair of the Air Jordan 3 North Carolina as her two favorites in the iconic line.

Exposure was another one of Williams’ many benefits as a member of the Jordan brand. Back in 2024, Williams featured in a campaign alongside French soccer player Youssouf Fofana. There, the former UConn star wore a special jacket with her name and the Jumpman logo adorned on the back.

Last year, Williams starred in Jordan Brand’s 40th-anniversary mini-musical ad directed by Wieden+Kennedy alongside NBA peers like Bam Adebayo and Doncic. And just last month, Williams debuted her custom player-exclusive version of the Jordan Heir Series 2 during a live fan event in Berlin with KICKZ.

Coming out of the Jordan bubble, Williams turned quite a few heads during this year’s WNBA All-Star weekend, which was a homecoming for the former Chicago Sky player. Partnering with her stylist Mariah Keopple, a professional ice hockey player herself, the Valkyries star wore one of Keopple’s own pieces for the orange carpet: a black resin corset and a high-waisted skirt with a dramatic, billowing train.

But Williams’ outfits can also fall on the opposite side of the spectrum, as was the case back in 2024. Ahead of a clash against the Phoenix Mercury, Williams decided to add humor to her pregame outfit by wearing a Kamala Harris shirt with the viral meme of her saying, “You think you just fell out of a coconut tree?”

With the Valkyries reaching the WNBA Finals in just their second season, the attention will be on Gabby Williams now more than ever. Especially after her performance in the semifinals against reigning champions Las Vegas Aces, a team that had been her kryptonite in the last few seasons. However, Williams stepped up this time, scoring 25, 20, and 16 points in three games to help her team sweep five-time MVP A’ja Wilson and company.

Williams was appreciated by all her teammates, as well as Jasmine Jordan, Michael Jordan’s daughter, who handles women’s sports marketing for the Jordan Brand. On her Instagram story, Jasmine tagged Williams to celebrate this accomplishment.

“Causeeee babbbyyyyy @gabbywilliams knows my heart and knowsss I be fallin asleepppppp mid game!
news.summary: From wearing jeans banned back in the league’s early years to the high-fashion and streetwear influence seen in players’ “tunnel fits” now, the WNBA’s current era is a major indication of how times have changed.

news.title: Trump Critics Keep Mocking Women in His Orbit Over Their Looks
news.text: Several prominent Donald Trump critics and partisan social media accounts have mocked the appearances of Barbera Thornhill, Susan Dell and Kimberly Guilfoyle in October. Newsweek contacted the U.S. Department of State via its media inquiries form for comment on Thornhill and contacted representatives for Dell and Guilfoyle via email on Wednesday. The remarks have renewed questions about how women’s looks become political ammunition, often eclipsing scrutiny of their work, conduct or qualifications. Appearance-based criticism has become a recurring feature of polarized American politics, spreading rapidly when photographs or videos of public figures circulate online. The latest posts also expose a bipartisan contradiction: allies condemn personal ridicule aimed at their own side while political leaders and commentators sometimes deploy it against opponents. Thornhill’s Appointment Prompts Personal Ridicule Thornhill was welcomed to the State Department on October 13 as Ambassador at Large to monitor and combat trafficking. The Senate confirmed Thornhill on August 7 as part of a group of nominees approved in a 51–47 vote. Her official portrait quickly circulated on social media, where some users questioned whether the image was genuine and others made disparaging remarks about her appearance. No verified evidence has established that the State Department photograph was digitally manipulated. Tim Miller, a former Republican strategist and prominent Trump critic, reposted the announcement with a line suggesting Thornhill would always keep her eyes open for traffickers. Anti-Trump X account Spiro’s Ghost responded with a GIF from the film Brazil depicting a cosmetic procedure. Those posts criticized Thornhill personally rather than addressing her credentials, though her background has separately attracted substantive scrutiny: Thornhill previously worked as a business executive and philanthropist, while anti-trafficking organization Protect All Children from Trafficking (PACT) questioned whether she had sufficient federal policy experience, the International Business Times reported. Susan Dell’s White House Appearance Draws Attacks Dell became the subject of similar commentary after joining husband Michael Dell and Trump at the White House on October 7 to discuss Trump Accounts, children’s investment accounts supported by the couple’s $6.25 billion commitment. Their pledge was designed to provide $250 to as many as 25 million eligible children. Posts included comparisons between older and recent images, along with references to “Mar-a-Lago face,” artificial intelligence and movie characters. Such remarks did not establish anything about Dell’s health or whether she had undergone cosmetic treatment, and no verified engagement data shows how representative they were of wider public opinion. The verified Liberal account Not Your Average Liberal shared one comparison under the phrase “The MAGA Effect.” Donald Trump's son, Eric Trump, condemned the treatment as “vicious attacks” on X, arguing that attention should instead be paid to the Dells’ philanthropy. Michael Dell also amplified messages thanking his wife and asking people to leave her alone, including posts from families who said their children had received $250 contributions. What Is 'Mar-a-Lago Face'? Some of the criticism has drawn on the phrase “Mar-a-Lago face,” a pejorative label that has emerged online and in media coverage for a particular beauty aesthetic associated with people in Trump’s political and social orbit. The term takes its name from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Florida. USA Today reported that plastic surgeons have described the aesthetic as including full lips, prominent cheekbones, very white teeth and limited facial movement. Other accounts have associated the phrase with conspicuous cosmetic procedures and heavily styled makeup. However, describing someone as having “Mar-a-Lago face” does not establish that the person has undergone cosmetic surgery, fillers or any particular procedure. Thornhill, Dell and Guilfoyle have not publicly confirmed whether or not they have undergone cosmetic surgery. Stephen King and John Oliver Target Guilfoyle The clearest examples involving nationally recognized Trump critics concerned Kimberly Guilfoyle. Stephen King, a well-known Trump detractor, posted a photograph of Guilfoyle on October 8 with the caption: “Under your bed... or in your closet...” The remark was widely interpreted and reported as mockery of her appearance. Comedian John Oliver also targeted Guilfoyle’s appearance while discussing separate allegations about her financial dealings with Trump donor Eric Deters on Last Week Tonight. After reading from messages that were reported to have been sent by Guilfoyle asking Deters for $100,000 toward an American Express bill, Oliver invented a parody continuation of the exchange, joking that she was also asking for money for Sephora and making a dig at her eyeliner, saying, "'Pumpkin, please send $100,000 to Sephora, I need a new vat of charcoal eyeliner. My style icon is a raccoon. Prayer hands,” per Variety. The underlying financial claim is separate. Deters alleged that Guilfoyle asked him to send $100,000 to her American Express account. Crucially, Deters said he did not make that payment. Guilfoyle’s attorney disputed the authenticity of the messages. Her attorney also said the money could have represented reimbursement for travel and speaking expenses, while Deters disputed that he owed Guilfoyle money. Appearance Attacks Cross Party Lines Criticism of these posts does not erase similar conduct from the political right. At a Tennessee rally on October 10, Trump sarcastically referred to former Vice President Kamala Harris as “beautiful.” He also repeatedly claimed that he is better-looking than Harris, The Independent reported. Gender and Appearance Have Long Collided In Politics The scrutiny facing women in Trump’s orbit fits into a much older pattern in American political life. Research has repeatedly found that women in politics receive disproportionate attention for their appearance and personal lives, even when reporting ostensibly focuses on their campaigns or public work. A 2020 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Communication, examining 90 studies involving more than 25,000 politicians and 750,000 news stories, found that women politicians received more attention to their appearance and personal lives than men. Researchers also found more negative coverage of women’s electoral viability and some evidence of stereotypical coverage of their traits and policy areas. That pattern stretches back decades. According to The Journalist's Resource, research on American elections in the 1980s found women running for Senate and governor received less coverage than male candidates, and that coverage was more negative. Later studies, per politicalparity.org, suggested the overall amount of coverage became more equal, but differences in what journalists focused on remained. One analysis of 2002 races found appearance mentioned in six percent of news stories about women candidates, compared with one percent of stories about men. The consequences are not completely straightforward. A separate experiment detailed in Who Cares What They Wear? Media, Gender, and the Influence of Candidate Appearance found that negative coverage of a candidate’s appearance reduced perceptions of professionalism for both men and women, rather than producing a greater penalty for women in that particular study. More broadly, however, a 2023 meta-analysis of 50 experimental studies involving more than 23,000 participants concluded that gender bias from political media coverage is conditional rather than universal. When differences did emerge from coverage about traits, appearance or family, researchers found that they mostly disadvantaged women by reinforcing stereotypes and lowering assessments of their viability and voting preferences. Appearance Attacks Are Not Limited To Women While women have faced distinctive appearance-based scrutiny in American politics, male politicians have hardly been immune from having their looks turned into political ammunition. One of the earliest television-era examples came during the 1960 presidential race. Richard Nixon, who had recently been ill and suffered a knee injury, appeared pale during his first televised debate against John F. Kennedy, while Kennedy appeared tanned and camera-ready. CNN's retrospective of the debate says Kennedy won the “image battle,” although the familiar claim that radio listeners preferred Nixon while television viewers favored Kennedy has subsequently been challenged. More explicit personal ridicule emerged during the 2016 Republican presidential primary. Trump repeatedly mocked Marco Rubio for sweating and called him “Little Marco.” Rubio retaliated by mocking Trump’s “small hands” and “spray tan,” telling supporters that Trump would “make America orange.” Chris Christie has also been repeatedly targeted over his weight. During a 2023 campaign appearance, Trump said of his Republican presidential rival, “Christie, he’s eating right now,” before telling an audience member not to call Christie a “fat pig.” Christie responded that millions of Americans struggled with their weight and criticized Trump for focusing on “the way I look.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Trump critics and partisan social media accounts have mocked Barbera Thornhill, Susan Dell and Kimberly Guilfoyle's looks.

news.title: Kamala Harris to campaign with governor candidate David Crowley
news.text:
WASHINGTON – Former Vice President and presidential candidate Kamala Harris will campaign with Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley later this month, according to his campaign.

The campaign visit scheduled for Oct. 26 will come a little over a week before Crowley and his opponent, Republican U.S. House Rep. Tom Tiffany, face off in one of most high-profile Wisconsin races on the ballot Nov. 3. Details about the visit have yet to be released.

The latest poll from Marquette had Crowley at a slight advantage over Tiffany, although some Republicans, like U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., argue that the polls writ-large are skewed left.

High-profile visits like these are seen as final closers as both campaigns pull out all the stops ahead of November. Crowley attended a fundraiser with Harris and actor Sean Penn in California last month.

More: David Crowley welcomes campaigning with Kamala Harris, Francesca Hong

Last week, former President Barack Obama, the nation's first Black president who won Wisconsin twice, endorsed Crowley in a video posted Oct. 8, in which he compared Crowley's background to his own. If elected, Crowley will be Wisconsin's first Black governor.

President Donald Trump has also issued his influential endorsement in the governor's race, announcing he was backing Republican candidate Tom Tiffany in January. Most recently, Trump alluded to a potential Wisconsin visit in a Truth Social post on Oct. 7.

Trump won Wisconsin in 2016 and 2024.

Harris' visit comes amid rumors about her potential 2028 presidential bid, which she hasn't publicly ruled out.

Harris is hardly a stranger to Wisconsin. In 2024, she visited Wisconsin four times in her role as vice president and frequently as the Democratic presidential candidate, including stops in Milwaukee, Madison, La Crosse and Big Bend in Waukesha County.

In that campaign season, in which Harris rose to the Democratic nomination after President Joe Biden's late exit from the race, the presidential nominees and their running mates made more than 40 visits to Wisconsin between mid-July and the November election.
