news.title: High school girls storm off at cross country race in protest against male runner who switched from boys' team
news.text:
A dozen high school cross country runners found themselves on the front lines of the transgender athlete debate at a meet in Washington on Tuesday.

The teenage girls from Camas High School in Camas, Washington, defiantly refused to compete on October 13 after discovering that they were being pitted against a biological male athlete.

Logan Mihailoff, a junior at Camas High, switched from the boys' competition to the girls' midseason, competing in the male field as recently as September 5. 

The switch sparked outrage among parents and students with a large group of the female Camas runners deciding to take a stand.

Almost half of the girls competing in Tuesday's race walked off the course in protest of the biological male's participation. 

When the horn blared, the transgender competitor and the remainder of the female runners took off but around 11 girls slowly walked past the starting line with their arms linked and into the nearby tree line, exiting the course and the race. 

Their bold move saw them sacrifice one of their high school competitions. However, their decision was supported by their parents, many of whom attended the race with signs calling to keep men out of women's sports. 

'The more I heard about her friends wanting to do something, the more I heard about her team wanting to do something, we definitely were in support of that,' Kevin Burns, the father of one of the protesting girls, Holly, told OutKick. 'We told her, do what you think is best.'

'You hear about it, but you just never think it's going to be on your kid's small cross-country team,' Holly's mother Sarah added. 

Mihailoff has run in boys' races as recently as last month. They competed in the junior varsity boys' race at the Ultimook Race in Oregon, finishing 76th out of 301 runners on September 5, according to The Columbian. 

Just over a month later on October 10, Mihailoff finished the second-fastest member of the Camas High girls' team in the women's elite race at the Nike Hole In The Wall XC Invitational in Arlington. 

Mihailoff ran a personal best time of 18 minutes, 36.8 seconds, which saw them finish 39th in the race, which features elite high school athletes from across the Northwest. 

'I don't see how it's OK to discriminate against my daughter and the daughters of everyone else that is trying to fairly compete,' Kevin Burns said.

Kevin and Sarah said that they were challenged by security when they attempted to hold up the signs protesting against transgender athletes competing in sports. 

They also claimed that they faced backlash from a woman, who confronted them during the race.

'I had a lady that came up to me and said she was a psychiatric nurse and that I was a disgusting human for holding up this sign and that I was doing psychological damage to these children,' Sarah said. 'I told her that one day I'm gonna have to stand before my Lord and Savior and I'm gonna feel good about this.' 

The protest comes less than a month before Washington voters are set to head to the polls to cast their ballot on an initiative to ban transgender athletes from women's sports. 

The state will vote on Initiative 638 on November 3, which, if passed, would ban biological males from competing in girls' K-12 sports.

It took hundreds of thousands of signatures from across Washington to get the measure on the ballot. 

And, despite being an overwhelmingly liberal state, there is optimism among activists that the initiative could pass. 

Tentative new local polling has reportedly shown that Washington voters will cast their ballots in favor of passing the ban. 

Polling conducted by Let's Go Washington, a conservative-backed political action committee that advocated for the proposed ban, earlier this month shows 56 percent of the vote going in favor of the ban in November, according to KUOW. 

'People are with us, and they don't wanna say it out loud,' Hallie Herzberg, a spokesperson for Let's Go Washington, told the outlet. 'They don't want to be villainized for it. They will support us, and they will stand up for girls, but they will do it in the safety of their own ballot.'

Meanwhile, nationally 66 percent of Americans are said to support policies that force trans athletes to play on sports teams that 'match their sex at birth,' according to polling that the Pew Research Center published last year.

Voters trend towards supporting banning trans athletes from competing with cisgender girls after they read the language used to describe the initiative as it will appear on the November ballot, according to Andrew Villeneuve, the founder of Northwest Progressive Institute, which has conducted some additional polling on the matter.

However, Democrats have conducted limited polling on the matter with party spokesperson Stephen Reed telling KUOW that, 'This is not a slam dunk like some folks think it might be.'

27 states have already passed policies that separate biological males from competing in women's sports in K-12. However, all of those policies were passed by state legislature rather than the popular vote.

Therefore, should Washington pass the initiative in November, it would become the first state to enact the policy through voter approval, according to Fox News.

Furthermore, it would also become the first state that Donald Trump lost to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election to adopt such a policy.

The President signed an executive order in February 2025 aimed at keeping trans athletes out of girls' and women's sports.

Washington outright rejected the order with the state's Superintendent Chris Reykdal immediately speaking out against the policy.

Reykdal said in a statement that the order tried to force schools to 'discriminate against trans female athletes' in exchange for federal funds, and that it sought to 'restrict transgender girls from participating in girls' sports with their peers.'

He called the order unlawful, saying it contradicted the Washington Law Against Discrimination and state school rules. He added: 'Our state law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and we will not back down from that.
news.summary: The teenage girls from Camas High School in Camas, Washington, defiantly refused to compete on October 13 after discovering that they were being pitted against a biological male athlete.

news.title: Mark Cuban: 'I'd Get Rid of All Political Parties'
news.text:
Today's guest is Mark Cuban, the billionaire entrepreneur and former Shark Tank star who is now on a mission to reform the American healthcare system. Through his companies, Cost Plus Drugs and Cost Plus Wellness, Cuban is trying to make healthcare more affordable by cutting out middlemen and making pricing more transparent. But he argues that fixing America's healthcare system will require breaking up massive conglomerates that wield enormous power over pricing and competition, often at the expense of patients.

Nick Gillespie talks with Cuban about why he supports bipartisan legislation from Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley to break up Big Medicine. Cuban explains how artificial intelligence can expose hidden costs in health insurance contracts and transform the way doctors diagnose and treat patients. They also discuss Cuban's support for Texas Democrat James Talarico and his belief that political parties have outlived their usefulness. The billionaire entrepreneur makes the case for restricting social media algorithms for children under 16 and discusses why he isn't particularly worried about socialism's growing popularity among young people. Finally, Cuban reflects on how Ayn Rand's The Fountainhead shaped his understanding of capitalism and why he believes helping others is part of being a successful entrepreneur.

4:13—Healthcare conglomerates and "contractual terrorism"

15:39—Drug pricing and pharmacy benefit managers

26:58—How AI will transform healthcare

33:04—The Trump administration's policy reforms

34:22—How does Cost Plus Drugs work?

43:08—The backlash against billionaires

47:52—Political parties and Texas governance

55:11—Would Cuban back a social media ban for minors?

55:50—The influence of Ayn Rand

This is an AI-generated transcript. Check all quotes against the audio for accuracy.

Nick Gillespie: This is The Reason Interview With Nick Gillespie. Thanks for listening, watching, however you're consuming this. My guest today is Mark Cuban, the former majority owner of the Mavericks, now a minority owner, if memory serves. And that's partly because you're going all in on Cost Plus Drugs, a company and a business model about prescription drugs and, more broadly, wellness and health care. We're going to talk about that in a little bit, but right now, you have recently in a very tight Texas Senate race, you've endorsed James Talarico, or you're speaking with him, partly because he has talked about coming up with a health care plan that you think will reduce health care costs. Can you talk a little about the Talarico plan and why that was so important for you in terms of signing on to appear with him?

Mark Cuban: I mean, really, what we agreed on is that we need to pass Elizabeth Warren's and Josh Hawley's Break Up Big Medicine Bill. And that was the fundamental reason why I supported him. I mean, there are other reasons as well, but I think that as long as we have these huge conglomerates that dominate the economics and provision of health care, the system's not ever gonna work, and we're gonna get what we have right now.

So, identify what is the main problem with health care right now? Is it just that everything costs too much, and that's because of the big conglomerates? Or is it that the quality of care is no good, the rate of innovation is dying? 

What's the main problem with health care?

It's the economic side. I mean, the U.S. has the best health care in the world. It's not even close. The problem is, it's not accessible to everybody, but it's not affordable to most. And that is underpinned by how the biggest conglomerates in the country, that do hundreds of billions of dollars each in revenue each year, dominate the economics of health care.

So how is the Break Up Big Medicine Act or bill how is that gonna actually reduce costs? Because I know in the past you've talked about being a small-l libertarian. You're obviously very much in favor of capitalism. You don't hate billionaires. You don't like wealth taxes. You like free markets. How is the Break Up Big Medicine Act gonna work? Because one of the reasons we're where we are now is because of all of the past government intrusions into the market or structuring of the market. I mean—

No, that's wrong…OK, let's just…

I mean, the government already spends about 50 cents of every dollar in the healthcare ecosystem. So it's not like this is a market, right?

Well, it's not a market. You're correct though. Right? But in order to have an efficient market, you have to have price discovery. In order to have price discovery, you can't have gag clauses in every single contract that every single health care—you can't have gag clauses in every single health care benefits contract that's signed. Period. End of story.

And who commands those gag clauses? The big companies that need to be broken up. And it's not an issue of what the government is doing. It's specifically an issue of the choices that are being made by the CEOs and C-suites of those companies.

You look at the largest vertically integrated health care companies: 3,000-plus subsidiaries, $150 billion in intercompany transfers. That's more than the GDP of 13 states. And so they literally dominate the economics. And that's just one company.

If you go to the top three, the point of this is, the leverage is not with the federal government in this particular case. The definitions, the relationships, the pricing, the rules are being set by these big conglomerates. And if you were to break them up, it would change.

Ok, so we can work through a more specific example. What's the worst conglomerate, then, or the biggest healthcare—vertically integrated provider? And how are they bilking everybody—customers, doctors, hospitals, unless they own the hospital system? Who's the worst, and how is that working?

UnitedHealthcare. They're the ones that have thousands of subsidiaries, $150 billion, $160 billion in intercompany transfers. They either contract or employ more than 10 percent of the doctors in this country.

Out of those 3,000 subsidiaries, they own pharmacy benefit managers, they own health care providers, they own what they call ASOs, third-party administrators that administrate care. They own Medicare, Medicaid, MCOs that manage Medicaid for states. There's just—I can't even begin to start to list all the different things that they control.

So one of the ideas behind a vertically integrated company is that they— if you are sourcing your own cost inputs, you can do things more efficiently, and you pass that on to the customers. So McDonald's grows its own potatoes because—

Sure, I know I get it. I know the potential benefit. Yeah.

Oh, no, no. I know that. So explain—

It's also a choice. So, here's the choice. You can pass it on and say, "Look, we're going to be more efficient and pass on the benefit of our efficiency." And the easy way to understand whether that's occurring—there are two easy ways.

One, to ask anybody who uses their services or any of their peers, and just ask them: Have you felt like you've been the beneficiary of their scale?

Based on the polls going around for these midterms, right, the number one issue is affordability, and the number one underpinning of that affordability is the cost of health care.

Number two, being a healthcare geek, I will read the transcripts of their quarterly earnings conference calls. The one thing I have yet to ever hear them say over the past four or five years is that, "Based on this investment, based on this new technology, based on this acquisition, we are going to be able to reduce the cost of care or services to patients that receive that care." Not one.

So patients just don't show up in the way you're talking about it? It's like… 

Not at all.

We've streamlined like our costs—

Right. Well, not even necessarily streamline our costs, but what does show up is: "We are going to be able to increase our earnings along with our previous trend. We are going to be able to increase our margins and our revenue for specialty medications," right? There's just a long list of things that they are pushing.

And the bottom line of this—and every capitalist, every CEO has to decide who they're responsible to. Typically, in a public company, which all of these are, they're responsible to shareholders. And that's not necessarily a bad thing if they're aligned also with their customers, their ultimate customers. It may not be the direct customer, but the ultimate customer, which is a patient.

They are not aligned. Not only are they not aligned with the patients, they're not aligned with any other stakeholders.

When you talk to corporations, big or small, a solo entrepreneur, 100 employees, 100,000 employees, and you say, "How are your health care costs doing these days? Are they going down? Are they going up?" And obviously, the response is they're going up.

And you talk to their members, their employees, their families: Are your deductibles and premiums going up or down?

And so the proof is in the pudding that they're aligned with their shareholders, but they are not aligned with their ultimate customers. And that creates a disconnect. And those are the decisions that they've made. In one case, with a tragic outcome, unfortunately.

And so going back to the Break Up Big Medicine Bill and the outcome, when you have somebody who is that big and has that much control and that much regulatory capture, it's AT&T time. It's Standard Oil time, again.

Yeah, I mean, but then it gets complicated. And I don't want to spend too much time on this, but in the sense that when Standard Oil got broken up, they were actually charging the least for their products in their history.

This should be easier then, right? Because now these guys are charging the most.

No, no. Well, I'm saying it gets complicated because you mentioned regulatory capture, and this is part of the problem. Like, if UHC, if UnitedHealthcare is so bad, why do companies keep using them as a benefit?

I'm so glad you asked that. Why do they keep on buying from them, right? Why do they keep on doing business with them? Right?

So I spend most of my days going to CEOs and explaining to them how they're getting ripped off and how they are getting worse outcomes by dealing with these big conglomerates. Almost all my days. And what I can tell you—

I'm sorry to interrupt, just real quick, because just to get you on the record on this. You're not against bigness per se…

Right? Big conglomerates—because people like Elizabeth Warren often are like, if it's a big company, break it up, right?

Not the issue to me at all.

If I were running that company, I'd be like, "We are so efficient. We are so good at what we do. We use AI and technology better than anybody, so good that we're pushing prices down." And because of that, we'll make more money.

And you know what? Even if we don't make more money, we'll make enough to keep our shareholders happy. But you know what? I'd rather be a great citizen of this amazing country of ours, and if that means better health care at less cost, and our P/E ratio needs to be a little higher to get that stock price where we want it, I'm good with that.

That's how I would—so I have no problem with scale.

The problem I have, like when you talk to people who work for these companies, when they say, "Yeah, I work for whoever," the first thing they say to me is, "I'm sorry. I need the job."

It's not like they're proud. It's not like, "Hey, we're doing such amazing things." And so that's the underpinning of all of this.

So go back to your point on why do companies hire them, right?

I spend so much of my time—literally before this call, I dealt with a group of people who were HR representatives and buyers of these services. And I said, "Do you like these companies that you're dealing with?"

They refer to the big insurance companies as the BUCAs, right? Blue Cross Blue Shield, United, Cigna, etc.

And they're like, "No, we don't like dealing with them."

I'm like, "Why do you?"

"Well, because our CEO just doesn't understand health care costs and health care benefits. And they may know somebody or do business with them."

Like, I've literally talked to humongous banks who have said that we're not going to switch because we'll lose their deposits and banking relationships.

Ok, that happens. So let's put them out.

So now I was talking to this group today, and I started giving examples of places where those big companies were taking advantage of them. And I went directly to contracts because most of the contracts are comparable.

So I call them contractual terrorism.

The city of Dallas, we'll use them as an example. Their pharmacy benefit manager contract: 1,300 pages. There's no human or humans or enough coffee on the planet.

I don't even know if the AIs are capable of scanning that.

Well, the AIs are capable of doing it, right? You kind of got ahead of me there, because before they were able to push things through.

So, like, for pharmacy benefits, there are these things called rebates, where the manufacturers give money back to the pharmacy benefit managers, and they have the choice of how to distribute it from there depending on the contracts, right?

And one of the biggest sources of rebates is something called specialty drugs. They're supposed to be more complicated drugs. Just as often, they're not, but they call them specialty.

But in these contracts, and I literally asked the question of this group who has a good understanding of their contract, I said, "How many of you have a clause in your contract that says specialty rebates, specialty medications either get a flat rebate or no rebate?"

They all raised their hands.

And then I said, "In that contract, doesn't it also say that that PBM owned by that big BUCA—"

That's the pharmacy benefit—

Benefit manager, right, gets to determine what is a specialty drug or not. So in some cases, it could be generic, it could be a little pill, and they call it a specialty drug so that they get to arbitrage the rebate or to retain the rebates instead of sharing them.

So going back to the question of why would a company do this, and it's even worse on the medical side. That's the pharmacy side.

There's no company that, if you work for a company that's self-insured, and God forbid you need to get some major surgery, and so they send you a bill, not even specifically to you, but for the whole company every week or every month, right? And the company just writes the check for the bill, and they may or may not even get examples of the claims so they can reconcile them to what was actually charged or paid to the hospital.

So you have these huge companies that have no way of reconciling whether or not what they were charged is what was paid to the hospital or doctor or provider.

So I was like, why do you do this? Why are you letting yourselves be taken advantage of? And it's because, "Well, it's just happened, it's changed so rapidly, and the prices have gone up so rapidly. We're still in the contract. We're still doing it."

And I'm like, so let me give you the way to resolve this. And this goes back to AI.

So what I've done, and I've done it for my companies, I've helped other companies do the same, I've helped states do the same. Now, with AI where it is, and it's only recently capable of doing this, you can take a 1,300-page contract. You can take a 600-page contract, and I tell them, take the PDF file of all of your health benefits contracts and put them into your favorite large language model and just use this prompt: "Where are they ripping us off?"

And within five minutes, you'll see, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Because it's contractual terrorism. They only have to squeeze through a couple of things that the lawyers don't see, and that changes the whole contract, and everything economically references the contract.

So part of, I mean, in any kind of market that's not working well, price signals are arbitrary or buried. There's a lack of transparency. People don't know what they're paying for, what all of the benefits are, how much they cost, and things like that.

There's also, and I know you've talked and written about this, where it's exacerbated by the fact that the company, I mean, a health benefit, it's not what your main company is doing. They're offering it for a variety of reasons. And this goes back to World War II or wage and price controls and things like that.

You know, whatever my company…I don't even know what my—Reason Foundation, the nonprofit that publishes this podcast, I don't know what they pay monthly for my premium. And I barely know what my premium is.

And do you know what your deductible is? Do you know?

Yes, I do indeed. And I had a kid last year, so I'm always hap—

Let me ask you a question, over $1,500 a year?

Yes, for the overall, it's like $6,000.

OK, so $6,000. Have you ever been prescribed, or has anybody in your family been prescribed, a brand medication?

No, I gave up on brand medications a while ago. I always go for the—but what's your point?

No, my point is that brand medications without generics, right?

Right. Yeah, yeah.

So let's just take a drug like Xarelto. The list price of Xarelto, sold by J&J, is $600. The way the system is structured by these big BUCAs and their pharmacy benefit managers is such that during your deductible phase, you and pretty much everybody else, unless your company negotiated something different, have to pay the full retail list price for that medication.

That's insane. Now the question becomes, why does that happen?

And I'm going to explain to you, and this is way inside baseball, how pricing for brand medications is done in the United States of America.

We'll, excuse me, we'll take a drug like Xarelto because it's easy to understand and use. $600 list price. When J&J sells that to one of the three big wholesalers—there's three of them that control 95 percent of the pharmaceutical transactions—when they sell to that wholesaler, you know what they sell it to them for? List price, $600.

Sounds crazy. If they came on Shark Tank, Kevin would probably say, "Take them out behind the barn and shoot them," because it makes no sense that multihundred-billion-dollar companies don't negotiate a discount.

But they're lucky in that the brands will give them 5 percent back if they prompt pay and give them some data.

So now let's just say 5 percent from a $600 drug means the net cost to the wholesaler is $570. That sets the floor for what they can charge pharmacies because they're not going to sell it for less than they pay.

Now what happens next, then, is now a pharmacy has paid $570 for that drug. When you walk in, or any of your family members walk in, or anybody who works for the foundation walks in who has a comparable deductible, the pharmacy can't sell it to you for less than $570 because that's the charge.

Now that's ridiculous in and of itself because you know how much J&J actually nets, give or take, for that medication? It's not $570. It's about $300.

Their yield, their net revenue is about half of the list price. And so where does that delta, the $570 minus $300, where does that go? That goes to the pharmacy benefit manager.

Now, if this was a real market where they didn't have control because of their control of formularies and lives covered, then J&J and all the other brands in the same situation would then sell to the wholesaler at $310. Remember, their net yield was $300, so they'd make $10 more.

And remember, the wholesaler was selling to the pharmacy for no markup. They make their money on generics, right? So they could sell it for $320 to the pharmacy, and they'd make more. And then the pharmacy could sell it for $325 to you and your family or any underinsured or uninsured patient, and they'd make more.

So everybody would make more, but more importantly, more people would be able to afford their medications, and more people would be able to adhere.

So the question becomes, why does it not happen that way? Because in a capitalist society, people are going to act in their own self-interest. That's the beauty of capitalism.

People are always going to find shortcuts and disrupt so that I can get you something…

Right, wherever they can. So I'm going to tell you why it doesn't happen, right? Because those big PBMs owned by the big BUCAs, they control these things called formularies, and they control the formularies for 85 percent of people who receive pharmacy benefits.

And the formularies are the drugs that are covered by a particular plan?

Correct, correct.

And if your medication is not on that formulary or it's on a low tier, because you know in your tiers for your own health care, right, you might pay zero, $10, $50, coinsurance, whatever it may be.

Well, so these PBMs are saying to the brand manufacturer, they've told me this, that if they don't play the game this way, sell at list price and only give a 5 percent, don't do it at net, if they don't play the game that way, they will diminish their positioning on that formulary, not just for that drug, but for their entire portfolio.

It's the same reason Cost Plus Drugs doesn't have a lot of brands, because they've said the same thing: If you work with Cost Plus, then we will diminish your position on the formulary.

So two quick questions that I think will clarify what you're talking about. One is, where did the pharmacy benefit managers come from? They weren't always part of vertically integrated institutions, well let's start with that. PBMs have been around at least since the '60s, and the whole idea, and it makes sense, is like, we're going to arbitrage a lot of possibilities, and we'll sell more drugs for the people who are making them, and we'll sell them cheaper to the people who are buying them.

But really just processing claims. Right? Somebody, there's a prescription, and you have insurance—

Yeah, how do we go from there to, I mean, PBMs in a lot of ways, those are your white whale, right? That's what Cost Plus Drugs is going after. That's where you tend to—

The whole thing. They're not a unique company. They're part of these vertically integrated companies, right? So culturally, they are the same, right? Optum Rx has the same organizational culture as United, CVS, etc.

So how did they get there? Vertical integration.

And once an insurance company who already had X number of plans that they control now buys a PBM, what they say to the employer and Medicare Advantage plans, they'll say, well, let's just start with employers, right?

Self-insured employers. Sixty-seven percent of people who get insurance through their company get it through a self-insured employer. That's about 150 million, 160 million people, right? And so those all go through a PBM at some level.

And by being able to control that, plus Medicare Advantage plans, plus Part D plans for Medicare, they have such market dominance. It's like they have more customers than Amazon does.

And just imagine Amazon saying, "If you don't do business the A, B, or C way that I demand, we're not going to allow you to sell on Amazon. Or we're going to make it so that somebody has to make 15 searches to find you."

That's the equivalent of what these vertically integrated companies are using their PBMs to do.

Yeah, how does the Break Up Big Medicine Act specifically address this issue of vertical integration?

Well, it's breaking them up by definition, right?

So then what's the benefit. Right, how do we get the lower prices and all that, right?

And so without having the market dominance to define and threaten, to say, "Look, we're not going to work with you unless you do it our way. And if you don't do it our way, you're going to lose access to 180 million customers," it ends that.

Yeah. And it says things like, if you are a medical provider, you cannot own this type of company. So, I mean—

So then we can talk about medical loss ratio and all that. 

It tries to end vertical integration or limit vertical integration.

Limit vertical integration, right. Because once you get market—and there's another part that we haven't talked about that goes hand in hand with doing capitalism the right way.

So in order to have an efficient market, and you mentioned this, you have to have price discovery. In order to have price discovery, you have to have price transparency and some level of contractual transparency. Because if the prices are in the contract, then you have to have some transparency there.

You know the old Fight Club thing? The number one rule of Fight Club is you can't talk about Fight Club. The number one rule of pharmacy benefit manager and ASO and other contracts from these vertically integrated companies, their number one rule is you can't talk about them. They have complete gag clauses.

So they literally say that—well, I'll give you a better example.

TRICARE, that offers all the pharmacy benefits for all the people serving in the military, retirees as well, right? They have their plans and everything. And for certain of their plans, particularly if you're a retiree who lives off base, you don't live on a military base, then you have to order certain generics from Express Scripts slash TRICARE, and the copay is like $16.

Well, it's cheaper in many of those cases to buy from Cost Plus Drugs. Just proving the point that it's not necessarily getting the best price dealing with a bigger company.

But that's not the bad part. That's not the bad.

We still have no idea, none, zero, how much taxpayers pay for those same drugs because they prevent everybody from seeing it.

Elizabeth Warren said she was willing to go and sit in a SCIF in order to be able to look at those prices, and they refused to allow it.

And a SCIF is a secret room where you can read super top-secret documents.

Yes, right. And they still wouldn't show them to her.

And so here we are taking taxpayer money. And if they're doing such a great job, you would think they'd be proud of their pricing.

"Mark Cuban, you can't touch our pricing with Cost Plus. We want everybody to see that. We'll put you out of business"

Yeah. So, I mean, part of the idea is, like, if you introduce transparency into more markets and people understand what other people are paying, you get a more informed market, and innovation is going to happen, prices will probably come down.

What you're talking about, like if you're going to the city of Dallas and you're saying, "Hey, here's a way for you to push back on your benefits provider and maybe to shop for better things." Part of it is information, part of it is regulation, and something—when I think of two people I hate for different reasons, but with almost equal ferocity, it's Josh Hawley and Elizabeth Warren. Most of the time when they're talking, I'm like, "Hey, all I know is my freedom is going to end up on the cutting room floor," right?

But there's regulation, and then there is the ability of individuals to make choices, meaningful choices.

I guess you talk a lot about AI in very positive terms, and you've laid out one way in which AI might help by just making people capable of understanding documents, contracts that they're about to sign.

In this particular case, absolutely.

Yeah, what are the other ways that you think AI is going to transform and improve the quality and quantity of medicine and health care?

One is drug discovery.

We'll get to the point, I don't know when, where we'll be able to take genetic information about ourselves, if we choose to, and make that available to far more advanced artificial intelligence than we see today, and say, "Analyze this. Tell me what I should be concerned about." Or, "Here's everybody in my family. Let's compare it and look for deltas and see how we can use AI to improve our health or wellness."

Make, like, personalized medicine.

Yeah, I'll give you a perfect example, right?

I have to take Synthroid for a thyroid scenario. And I was taking iron supplements because I work out and I sweat a lot, and my iron levels were low. I had no idea you couldn't take them at the same time. None. My doctor didn't know because you can't remember everything. And so I put it into Claude, and boom, I found out you've got to take them at least four or five hours apart.

Simple, simple, simple example.

We're all using Dr. ChatGPT and Dr. Claude to a certain extent. Doesn't make them perfect, doesn't make them accurate in all cases, but it gives us access to this information we otherwise didn't have.

But to go back to your question, as AI gets more advanced, not only will we be able to use it for personalized medicine, but it's capable of memorizing everything.

Now, AIs don't know the consequences of their actions. AIs don't have ethics, right? AIs are not smart. They're just able to combine things in ways that they've seen before or ways that you tell them to do. But within that constraint, doctors will be able to use them to more efficiently and effectively make determinations about somebody's health. So I see it as a big positive as long as we all understand that there are certain things that they can't do.

I'll give you one more example.

The minute an AI is released, we're done training and it's made available to the world, it's out of date.

This brilliant conversation you and I are having right now, no AI knows about. And even if it's published, unless you publish a transcript along with it, it has no way to consume the video itself.

So there's always built-in latency. And so because of that, it's always going to be behind.

And you talk about a capitalistic system and how people adapt. Well, researchers and doctors who publish are recognizing that, "Hey, maybe it's smarter that I don't publish, I don't try to patent this particular device or approach to solving a health care problem. Instead, I'll just keep it to myself and either sell it to a company that can benefit from it or put it in my own model."

And so that means you're going to have disparate information in different models.

AI is probabilistic. It's not deterministic. You're not going to ever get a scenario where you put something in four different models and you get the exact same answer.

So within health care, we have to understand those constraints. And by understanding those constraints, we can use the tools to our benefit. And I think that improves health care in a thousand different ways.

Let's talk a little bit about the regulatory framework. Donald Trump and Robert Kennedy, secretary of Health and Human Services, talked, particularly for round two, or the second term for Trump, talked a really big game about changing the regulatory apparatus at places like the FDA.

It costs anywhere from a billion to several billion dollars, might take more than 10 years, to bring a drug to market. By the time it comes to market, part of its patent life is already over, et cetera, and things like that.

Are there regulations, are there policy changes that the Trump administration has made that you're bullish on, that you think were in a right direction?

I think with things like biosimilars, which are effectively injectable generics, they removed one of the steps, which I thought was smart. Because having that, I forget the exact terminology, my partner knows this stuff better than I do, but having that third-tier trial to confirm what you already know is going to happen, and there haven't been any exceptions to prove that you need it, I thought that was really smart.

But I don't get involved in the FDA side in depth as much as I do on the commercial side.

Right. Well, let's talk about Cost Plus Drugs and explain the mechanics. Before this, I went to—and of course, because he has to put his name on everything, Trump started a prescription program online, TrumpRx. It's a government program where you can get coupons, basically, for things.

One of the drugs that I take is an off-patent statin, and it used to be known as Crestor, right, when it was on patent. And I looked up on the TrumpRx plan, it would cost me $8.60. And then I went to Cost Plus, and it said it would be $5.66. This is for a 30-day supply, 10 milligrams. And then I'm on Cigna, and it costs me zero when I fill that prescription.

But it doesn't cost you zero, right? You're paying it.

Yeah, absolutely right. And unfortunately, it costs my colleagues something. They chip in a little bit as well. But how does Cost Plus— how does it work? If you go there and you already have insurance, how do you use it in a way that you know what you're going to pay for a drug, and it's probably going to be cheaper?

So two different paths, right?

So if you have insurance, then if you work with one of the big PBMs, the big three PBMs, you're not going to be able to use your insurance with Cost Plus Drugs.

There are about 35, give or take, pass-through PBMs that we partner with. So if you have insurance cards from them, you just go in there and click on insurance, and you put in the card ID, and you get the benefit. It's probably going to be a zero copay, but we'll ship it to you, right? Because that's the benefit of sorts.

If you happen to be somebody who is on a Medicare Advantage plan and are prescribed a drug that's not covered, it's not on your formulary, or there's a high copay or high coinsurance, that's a perfect customer for us because you can come to us. We're far less expensive, including shipping and handling and everything, and you use us to save money.

And if you're in one of eight states, Tennessee, Texas, and a few others, then you can also count that against your deductible.

If you're completely uninsured, then we're a godsend for you, particularly if it's an expensive medication, and particularly now with biosimilars. So now there's a biosimilar for Humira. There's a biosimilar for Stelara. Last year, Stelara would have cost you or your employer or somebody $127,000. Now our cost is $365 plus shipping.

Yeah. What limits the types of drugs that you offer? Because I noticed, I think when I looked today, there were no GLP-1s, right? You don't do things like Adderall or the generic versions of Adderall. Explain why those are—

On controlled substances, we just don't want to fight the battle, right? Because there are just too many risks, and we wanted to make sure that we weren't in a position of contributing in ways we didn't want to contribute.

In terms of GLP-1s and brand medications and specialty medications, as I referred to earlier, the big PBMs have gone to the brand manufacturers, specialty manufacturers, and told them, "If you deal with Cost Plus Drugs, we will diminish your positioning on our formulary."

Now the question becomes, why? Why do these huge conglomerates care about us?

Well, there's a study that's getting ready to come out that says every area of health care costs has gone up over the past 30 years, except starting in 2022, the cost of generics started to level off and then started going down.

That's when we launched, January of 2022.

And the reason that happened, and the reason these big PBMs and conglomerates are afraid of us, is because when you go to Cost Plus, you put in your statin, right? And we showed you our actual cost, and then we showed you our markup was only 15 percent.

And so if we were to do the same thing with brand drugs, all of a sudden, all that premium, remember we talked about the pricing of brand medications, all that premium margin that is going to PBMs to keep or distribute would be gone.

Because everybody would finally know the actual cost, just like they know the actual cost of biosimilars and specialty generics and general generics, like you saw.

Do you think, in a market sense, is the function of Cost Plus, obviously, is to sell drugs or deliver them to people who need them at prices they're willing to pay or want or can afford, but is part of it also that it disciplines the big guys? Because if what you're saying is true, they're going to have to start taking into account that if we keep squeezing this stone—

So then where are the limits of that effectiveness? When I mentioned Standard Oil, at its peak market share, was selling its products for the least amount. It was because they had a monopoly. They had over 90 percent of market share in home heating oil and lighting and things like that. But they acted as if they were constantly about to be…

Go out of business.Yeah, yeah…

Right. So, I mean, where are the other places in the medical industry? In recent essays, and preparing for this, you said, well, it's not the pharmaceutical companies, because they're often—

They're not innocent, but they're not the worst—

Yeah, ok. It's not the doctors. It's not the government. But when I look at it, it's like the American Medical Association and other groups that govern the number of medical licenses that get issued every year or the number of resident beds that are available. They're not doing anything to increase supply.

No, I agree. I'm not saying I agree with that, right? But the AMA is not a government entity either.

Well, it's quasi, right? Because you have to show—but I'm saying, how do you bring that same kind of market force, that kind of comp….This is like real competition to say, "You know what? My competitor, who's got 90 percent market share, is selling something for $10 a unit. I'm going to sell it for $8 a unit, and I'm still doing well, and you're making out better, and they're going to have to change." How do you bring that to bear on the larger healthcare system?

Because what it's missing is not only price, but trust. Nobody trusts the economic side of health care. You don't. I don't care who you are, right? Every poll, everything says…right.

I look at trust as a formula: Trust equals transparency divided by self-interest.

We're completely transparent. We show our costs. We're still the only pharmacy that publishes a price list. We have a programming interface where anybody can pull down our pricing anytime they want.

So we're completely transparent there, and we only mark up 15 percent. So that's fair, right?

And so that's what differentiates us to start, right? So people can work with us, and they trust our pricing. They know what it is.

We charge the same price to everybody, no matter who you are, where you are, what time of day it is. It doesn't matter.

When our volumes go up, like with TrumpRx, it's a portal. As you saw, you can come find your way to us. Our volumes went up. Our costs went down.

At Cost Plus, we pass those cost cuts on to our patients. We were able to lower the price of 190 more drugs. And so we're able to start with these drugs, right? We're also getting involved with manufacturing. We manufacture drugs that are sterile injectables that are on the FDA short supply list.

We also have used AI and used robotics to shrink the size of our initial manufacturing plant from football-field size, so about 5,000 square feet. And over the last five years, we've been able to shrink that into the size of a tractor-trailer.

We call them pods. And these pods are going to be our biggest business. They're our most disruptive business because we've been able to combine AI and technology so that we can take these little things, tractor-trailer size, and ship them anywhere.

Ecological disaster, weather disaster, God forbid, war disaster, we can put them there and, depending on what kind of pod it is, make any kind of drugs.

And because we can daisy-chain these things together, we're able to manufacture in volume so that we can manufacture generic tablets cheaper than we can buy them from India.

So then let me, and this might seem like a leap, but in what you just described, and particularly the trust divided by self-interest, all of what you're talking about, all this innovation, why do people—or let me say this: If there's anything that's less popular than data centers and AI, it's billionaires like yourself.

What you just gave is a riff that is, if you believe in free minds and free markets, that's been Reason's catchphrase for decades, this is beautiful. And you're describing exactly how the system should work.

But we have, in contemporary America, people, including people like Elizabeth Warren, the governor of California, who want billionaire taxes. There are members of Congress who have staff members who say every billionaire is a policy failure.

Where is the anger? And when I say people like you, there aren't that many billionaires, but in terms of economic innovation and people doing well, it seems like it's worse now.

If you can't pay your rent, if you can't pay for your medications, if you can't pay for daycare, if you can't pay for food, you're just mad.

And when you're mad, you're not looking to say, "Ok, let me find a logical construct to define why I should be mad or why I'm in these circumstances." You're just mad.

And when you're mad like that, and I've been broke, right? Six guys living in a three-bedroom apartment, et cetera, no money in the bank. You're just mad at whoever is a convenient target.

And so I don't begrudge them. Hopefully, they'll eat me last.

I understand why politicians say billionaires are a policy failure because we're an easy target. I don't blame them for doing it that way. But as an entrepreneur, I'm still going to do what entrepreneurs do. It's why I did Shark Tank for 15 years, because I wanted people to be excited about being an entrepreneur. I wanted them to see, when they watched the show and somebody walked in on that carpet from Idaho or Iowa or wherever with nothing, they had a chance for their American dream to come true. 

And if they can do it, I wanted them to think, "I can do it."

And so do you feel like that dream is still alive? Or is it, because when people talk about, ok, it's hard to make rent, it's hard to do this, it's hard to do that. All of this struggle is always real. But is it just that that's the struggle? I mean, are things worse now than they used to be?

No, they're not necessarily worse, right? But we communicate differently now than we did before. Each of us is on social media at some level, whether we know it or like it or not. And each of us gets our own unique feed on social media.

There's no more Walter Cronkite. There's no more Dan Rather, where we all have communal shows that we all watched and basically understood and agreed on some level.

And there's a reason why, right? I mean, those disappeared partly because they weren't really giving people what they wanted, right?

Regardless of what it was, technology is technology. It's going to find its place, right?

I mean, I started the very first streaming company because people didn't have access to, in my case, Indiana basketball or music or whatever it may be, shows.

So people want more, but what's changed dramatically is how algorithms distribute content to each of us individually.

We all get our own individual feed on each of our social media platforms. Mine's not like yours, and they're like snowflakes. No two are alike.

And because of that, engagement increases with anger. And so every one of those algorithms has an incentive to make us mad.

Because the madder we get, the more we consume. The more we consume, the more ads that are sold. The more ads that are sold, the more subscriptions that are bought, et cetera, et cetera.

And because of that, if I'm mad about not being able to afford my rent, I'm mad about the cockroaches in the kitchen, I'm mad about the cost of beef, whatever it may be, you better damn well believe I'm getting a lot of that in my social media feed.

And if someone comes along and in that feed says it's this billionaire's or that billionaire's fault, what do you think I'm going to believe if that's 30 percent of the content I consume in any given day?

That's what's changed dramatically. And I say this all the time: Whoever controls the algorithm controls a lot of people.

Yeah. You have, in the 2024 election, I believe you're a political independent, but you came out and talked about how you wanted Kamala Harris to win. You were backing her. You're backing Talarico against Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate. There's, of course, Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate, who looks like he's going to cover the spread in Texas.

But I guess in terms of politics, at the state level, there's a real experiment going on. I'm talking to you from New York. New York City, New York state, and California are pursuing one model of governance, it seems, which is high tax, high regulation, high social services, or this is what they claim.

And then you have places like Texas and Florida that are saying we're going to do less tax, less regulation, we're going to give less services.

How do you feel about being in Texas? You've been there for decades now. It's your home place. Is Texas a better model compared to, say, California and New York state? Or how do you gauge that?

It's the ultimate capitalist decision, right? I mean.

Where you live.

Yeah, where do you live. And politicians, they sell what people will buy, what voters will buy.

And in terms of how I feel about Texas, when I got here, it was pretty much blue, and then it was purple, and then it was red, and it'll change again, just like multiple states, right?

What a conservative is today is far different than it was 11 years ago, you know? And the parties are completely different. If it were up to me, I'd get rid of all political parties. I think they've outlived their usefulness. They're just a way to raise money and to try to aggregate power as opposed to the power of ideas.

I don't give to politicians. I don't give a penny to politicians. Either you agree with what I have to say and you think it's of value to you, or you don't. And I have no intent of changing that.

Either my ideas stand up on their own, or they don't.

And in terms of my own philosophy here in Dallas, I'm an entrepreneur. And Dallas has been, Texas has been, great for me as an entrepreneur, been great for my family. I owe a lot to the city and the state, but it's changed radically, to use that term, over the years that I've been here.

Do you feel like it's getting better, getting worse, or it's just—

No, it's going to change no matter what.

The only constant is change.

My dad used to say, "You don't live in the world you were born into," you know? And it's the same thing here, where especially now with AI, I mean, there's always, like my kids, one was born before the iPhone, two weren't. Shit's going to change.

And so I don't look at it and say, "Well, pick this point in time, is it good? Is it bad?"

I look at it and say, "What can I do to make the world better?"

Look, I'm one lucky guy, right? My life is so much different than I ever possibly imagined.

And as an empathetic capitalist, right, as a compassionate capitalist, I want to give something back. My next dollar won't change my life, but it can change somebody else's life.

And when I talk to people about capitalism, that's the message I want to convey.

Now, if I was 25 again or 35 again and in healthcare, I'm sure I'd be trying to build as huge a company as I possibly could and sell it for as much money as I could because the one thing that I would want, the one thing I valued most, is time.

And the best way to gain control of your time is through your personal economics.

And so everybody's going to have their different perspective on where they live, how it's doing for them, what comes next. All I can do is try to help where I can help.

You mentioned being 25 again. Does the popularity or the kind of embrace of the idea of socialism, or the term socialism, concern you, particularly among Gen Z?

Explain that, because a lot of people are like, when you hear capitalism is at a kind of historic low in terms of positive feelings, socialism in America is at a historic high, why doesn't that concern you?

So I'll go back to the algorithms and social media again, right?

When I talk to—I have three kids who are now 17, 20, and 23. And I talk to them and their friends, and a couple of them are entrepreneurial.

And their friends will come on and give me all these ideas that they think are great businesses. And I've heard them all, right? You know, shoe drops, dropships. And I'm like, these are old, tired.

Where did you get these? Social media.

How do you understand how to run this business? Social media.

Where did you watch anything? YouTube, right? Or I saw it on Instagram.

So if you take that same concept toward business, the same thing is going to work when it comes to understanding political systems and politics in general.

Kids are getting short sound bites. And if somebody who's popular and goes viral says, "Hey, I just started this business. We're going to be selling widgets at 100 percent markup. That's socialism. I hate capitalism, but I do socialism business the right way," that's the way they're going to convey how they understand something.

We don't live in a world—if I have a problem with Gen Z, it's that they don't read books.

And it's not that they can't learn because AI can be a great democratizer of information. You can ask AI to teach you anything, and like a teacher, it's not always going to be right, but you have that opportunity to learn.

It's just we don't read and consume information the way we used to. And I think that makes it harder for kids to discern between fact and fiction, information and misinformation.

And I think that's the problem again when I—

That also changes with age, right? I mean, like—

Yeah, of course.

You start to figure things out.

Yeah, hopefully, right?

But we don't know, really, because Friendster was 2006 or whatever it was, and then Instagram became popular in 2011 with Snapchat, right?

So that's only 15 years of history, really. YouTube's been around longer, but the algorithms themselves really only started to hit in 2012.

And so we only have about 13, 14 years of history. So we don't know how kids are going to evolve through this period in their lives as they become older. We have no idea.

And so when I see Australia say, "Ok, 16 and under, ehh, no social media." Some people might say, "Well, that's wrong. We don't want government involved. Let the chips fall where they may."

I'm like, no. I really believe that people don't understand how algorithms work, and they don't understand how detrimental they are not only to a kid's mental health, but their ability to learn and how they perceive the world.

I think that's a real problem. Like when you see—

Would you back a law in America, in the U.S.? Say you would be in favor of a—

16 and under. 16 and under.

I wouldn't say ban them from social media, but I would say ban them from algorithmic access.

Now there's a problem because Section 230, on Instagram an algorithm is just as protected as any other website, right? So it's a challenge.

But if I could overturn that, or at least modify it, in a heartbeat.

Ok, so then final question. You mentioned reading books, being younger. You mention Ayn Rand a fair amount, or—

Howard Roark, baby. Howard Roark's my guy.

All right, yes. So then I'm wondering how Ayn Rand would think about the idea of the government saying, "Ok, here's an arbitrary age level that you can access information or not." But beyond that, talk a little bit about how you came to know Ayn Rand's work and why it was so important to you.

Oh, my mom. My mom was a housewife who had every odd job you can imagine, went through every pop psychology you can imagine.

And what did they call the people who followed Ayn Rand? I forget the name they gave.

Objectivists.

The Objectivists, right? So we used to get the Objectivism newsletter. There was a guy named Nathaniel Branden who was big in Objectivism, and he would have records, and my mom would play the records.

And so I would have all that just around me all the time. And she was a Democrat, a hard-core Democrat, by the way.

But at the same time, I remember reading The Fountainhead and just connecting to Howard Roark.

And then I remember reading The Virtue of Selfishness and thinking to myself, you know what? To me, being selfish means helping people because that's what makes me feel best. And that's what being selfish is all about, doing what makes you feel best.

And I didn't take it as, "Ok, laissez faire ideology is strategy in life." I took it as being an individual and finding your way and work your ass off. There's going to be issues, but respect other people who may not have the same opportunities that you do.

And it's not like I grew up with a silver spoon. My dad did upholstery on cars, never made more than $40,000, etc.

But I always looked at it as I can find the motivation in Howard Roark. I can't tell you how many times I read that book. I had to stop reading the book because I would get so fired up that people didn't like it.

You're going to blow up a building somewhere.

No, not like that, right? But for business, right? Because I get so intense when it comes to learning things for a new business, like with health care, whatever it may be, that people have to slow me down.

And so I literally had to stop reading The Fountainhead over and over again.

Wow, that's a great story. We're going to leave it there. Mark Cuban, thank you so much for talking to Reason. And I know I, for one, will keep looking at Cost Plus Drugs.

Please do. costplusdrugs.com.

Yeah, when it's cheaper, I'm going to be there.

Thanks for having me on. I really enjoyed it.

Thank you so much, Mark.
news.summary: Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban discusses breaking up Big Medicine, why he wants to abolish political parties, and how Ayn Rand shaped his views on capitalism.
news.author: Nick Gillespie

news.title: Kamala Harris Recalls the Time Husband Doug Emhoff Nearly Came to Blows with a Protester to Protect Her
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is opening up about a surprising time when her husband, Doug Emhoff, almost popped out and showed folks he wasn’t the one to play with when it comes to his wife. And funny enough, her story isn’t the only example out there!

Harris’ reveal came as part of her latest interview with Keke Palmer on the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” podcast. There, the two women spoke about how tough it is to warn their families about negative press, and how they urge them not to respond or get physical with people.

That’s when Harris shared that there was a past moment when her husband almost got involved in a physical altercation with a man years ago.

“That did happen once. Doug jumped the stage. Doug was in the back of the auditorium, and I was on the stage. And this fella came on the stage, approaching me. And Doug was in the back of the auditorium. [He] ran down the aisle, right down the middle, and jumped the stage. So that has happened,” Harris said around the 18-minute mark with a laugh.

After doing some digging, it’s highly likely that the former VP is referring to the 2019 incident that took place at MoveOn’s Big Ideas Forum in San Francisco. While speaking in her capacity as then-Senator, a man randomly bum-rushed the stage, took her mic, and began espousing his feelings on whatever cause he was there to represent.

Related: Stress, Regrets and Other Hot Tea From Kamala Harris’ Memoir Press Tour

It only took a few seconds before event staff, security, and Emhoff himself jumped onstage and forcefully got the man offstage. Check out the clip below.

But as we mentioned earlier, that was far from the only time Emhoff would stand 10 toes down for his wife. We all can’t forget how he gave Bruce Fischer, the husband of GOP Senator Deb Fischer, a taste of his own medicine in January 2025. For context, this was all spawned by Bruce’s refusal to shake then-Vice President Harris’ hand as she was swearing in his wife to office.

Weeks later, at the ceremonial tea at the White House, the former second gentleman opted not to shake Bruce’s hand at that event. As we previously told you at the time, Emhoff reportedly told him: “Why would you try to shake my hand when you wouldn’t shake my wife’s hand?” Bruce did end up eventually apologizing to Emhoff over the exchange, though he stopped short of issuing one to Harris herself.

It’s clear to see that Emhoff doesn’t play when it comes to respecting and protecting his wife. And honestly, we love to see it!

news.title: New Texas Senate poll shows where the race stands before early voting
news.text:
Texas voters are split on the U.S. Senate race heading into early voting, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico holding a narrow edge over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

The latest University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll shows Paxton trailing Talarico, 47% to 50%, within the poll’s 3.3-point margin of error, with 1% of voters preferring Libertarian Ted Brown and 2% preferring an unspecified “someone else.”

It's the latest in a string of October polls showing the race tightening in a state that last elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 1988.

Here's what the poll says and how it compares to other October polls.

James Talarico, Ken Paxton within Texas Senate poll's margin of error

The Texas Politics Project poll was conducted Sept. 25 to Oct. 5, with trial ballot results presented among a sample of 861 likely voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.

The poll found that both candidates are holding their partisan bases: 92% of Republican likely voters picked Paxton, and 98% of Democrats picked Talarico. Among those who recalled voting for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, 98% back Talarico. Among 2024 President Donald Trump voters, 89% back Paxton.

Trump has made several Texas campaign stops for Paxton in recent weeks, including Oct. 1 in Denton and Oct. 7 in San Antonio.

Talarico’s favorability ratings remain strong among Democratic partisans, according to the poll's analysis, with 92% viewing him favorably and 1% unfavorably, compared with Paxton’s among his Republican base, with 69% viewing him favorably and 15% unfavorably.

The poll also looked at how independents are breaking and found that independent likely voters prefer Talarico over Paxton, 69% to 11%.

The poll also broke out support by key demographic groups:

Recent Texas U.S. Senate race polls

news.title: Kamala Harris adds stops to her final midterm campaign stretch. Her decision about 2028 comes later
news.text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Kamala Harris is building out her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats, completing a midterm schedule that by Election Day will have taken her to multiple early presidential primary states on Democrats’ 2028 calendar as the former vice president mulls whether to seek the White House again.

Spanning from Oct. 21 to Oct. 30, Harris’ expanded closing stretch will now include New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Mississippi, along with a Florida virtual event, according to a schedule her office shared first with The Associated Press. Harris already had announced late October stops in Georgia and Nevada.

Harris has said in multiple recent interviews that she’s focused on helping Democrats win in November. But she’s not ruled out another presidential campaign after losing the 2024 general election to Donald Trump.

Her late October tour focuses on nominees for governor and U.S. Senate, including pairings that put the first Black woman to serve as vice president alongside potential history-making candidates.

Harris will open Oct. 21 in Nevada with Aaron Ford, the state’s first Black attorney general who would be the state’s first Black governor, and other candidates. She’ll also meet with Culinary Workers Union members. Nevada holds the second 2028 presidential nominating contest, after South Carolina.

On Oct. 22, she will be in Mississippi with Scott Colom, who would be the state’s first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom has recently begun to garner more attention from national Democrats as he faces Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

From Mississippi, Harris will head to New Hampshire on Oct. 24 to campaign with Senate nominee Chris Pappas and participate in a discussion on reproductive care and abortion rights. As vice president, Harris was the Biden White House’s foremost abortion rights advocate, especially during the 2022 midterm campaign. New Hampshire comes third in Democrats’ 2028 primary order.

Harris and Wisconsin gubernatorial nominee David Crowley will campaign together Oct. 26. Harris will finish with a three-day swing in Georgia that begins Oct. 28. She will campaign with Sen. Jon Ossoff, attend voter protection events and speak Oct. 30 at the Fulton County Democratic Party’s annual gala in Atlanta.

While in Georgia, Harris will headline a virtual organizing event with Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon, who would be her state’s first Black U.S. senator. That will put Harris, who hails from the Democrats’ liberal establishment, alongside one of the party’s most progressive nominees. A state lawmaker, Nixon identifies as a democratic socialist and draws support from many left-flank activists who in 2024 criticized Harris as too moderate.

The itinerary follows earlier in-person and online campaign appearances and fundraisers, along with voter protection and organizing events Harris helped lead, including for the Democratic National Committee. Most recently, Harris was in Michigan to campaign for Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — another notable progressive Democratic nominee — and speak at an NAACP event.
