news.title: US Midterm Elections 2026: 10 House Races That Could Decide Control of Congress
news.text:
The 2026 US midterm elections could reshape the political landscape in Washington. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for election, and the party that wins control will have a major say in the legislative agenda, government oversight, spending decisions, and investigations involving the Trump administration.

Democrats are hoping to capitalize on the historical tendency for the president’s party to lose House seats in midterm elections. Republicans, meanwhile, have pursued congressional redistricting in several states to improve their electoral position.

But changing district boundaries does not guarantee victories. Several districts Republicans sought to make more favorable to their candidates have become competitive, while incumbents in both parties face local concerns that could outweigh national political trends.

From New York and Texas to Iowa and Florida, the contests offer a snapshot of the issues shaping the campaign: the cost of living, immigration, allegations of misconduct, candidate fundraising, and voter attitudes toward the president.

Why Do the 2026 Midterm Elections Matter?

Midterm elections take place halfway through a president’s four-year term. Unlike presidential elections, they do not determine who occupies the White House, but they can change which party controls Congress.

The House has 435 voting members, and a party generally needs 218 seats for a majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the 2026 contest to secure control, according to the current race outlook. 

Control of the chamber matters for three main reasons:

Legislation: The House plays a central role in passing bills and determining federal spending priorities.

Oversight: The party in control influences committee leadership, congressional hearings, and investigations into the executive branch.

Political leverage: A change in the majority could complicate Trump’s legislative agenda and force greater negotiation between the White House and Congress.

Historical patterns provide Democrats with a reason for optimism, but they do not determine the result. Individual races will depend on local political conditions, candidate quality, turnout, campaign spending, and the issues voters consider most important.

How Is Redistricting Affecting the House Race?

Redistricting—the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries—has become a major part of the battle for the House.

Republicans have pursued changes in states including Texas and North Carolina, aiming to improve their chances of winning additional seats. Democrats have challenged those efforts politically and have sought opportunities in districts where the new boundaries have not produced the expected advantage. 

Texas is a particularly important example. Republican lawmakers redrew districts in 2025 with the goal of making several Democratic-held seats more favorable to Republicans. Yet shifting voter sentiment, including changing political attitudes among Hispanic voters in South Texas, has made some of those contests more competitive than Republicans had hoped. 

The outcome will depend on more than the shape of a district. Redistricting changes the electorate candidates must appeal to, but economic concerns, candidate performance, and voter turnout can still affect the result.

With control of the House potentially resting on a handful of seats, even small changes in competitive districts could have national consequences.

10 House Races to Watch in the 2026 US Midterm Elections

1. New York: Can Mike Lawler Hold His Seat?

Republican Representative Mike Lawler faces a difficult reelection contest against Democrat Cait Conley, a combat veteran and national security expert.

Lawler represents one of only three Republican-held congressional districts won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, making his seat a key target for Democrats.

Campaign finances add another layer to the contest. Democrats have spent more than Republicans in the district, while Lawler has maintained a substantial advantage in cash available to his campaign. Polls conducted in late September showed the candidates running closely, with neither establishing a decisive lead. 

The race will test whether Lawler can maintain support in a district that backed the Democratic presidential candidate in 2024 while Republicans seek to defend their narrow House majority.

2. Texas: Could Republican Redistricting Backfire?

Texas is one of the most consequential battlegrounds in the fight for the House because Republicans redrew congressional districts in an effort to improve their chances of winning additional seats.

Three of the districts identified in the supplied race analysis have become competitive, including contests involving Democratic Representatives Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar, as well as a race between Republican Carlos De La Cruz and Democrat Johnny Garcia.

Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores, a former Texas Army National Guard infantry captain and former assistant US attorney. Gonzalez has held a fundraising advantage, while Democratic spending to defend the seat has exceeded Republican spending to win it, according to the reported figures. 

The underlying question is whether redrawn boundaries will be enough to overcome local political shifts. South Texas has become a closely watched region because changes in support among Hispanic voters could influence several contests.

For Republicans, the stakes extend beyond individual incumbents: winning these districts could help offset losses elsewhere. For Democrats, keeping the races competitive could limit the gains Republicans hoped to achieve through redistricting.

3. North Carolina: Don Davis Faces a Tougher Map

Democratic Representative Don Davis is seeking reelection against Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel.

Republican redistricting changed the political makeup of Davis’s district, making it more favorable to Trump in the 2024 presidential election than it had been previously. That shift could make Davis’s reelection campaign more difficult.

Davis has reported stronger fundraising and cash reserves than Buckhout, while Democrats have invested substantially more in the race than Republicans, according to the supplied figures. A poll released in the week covered by the original report gave Davis a 10-point lead. 

The contest illustrates the distinction between a district’s presidential voting history and its congressional preferences. A district that favors one party at the presidential level does not automatically elect a candidate from that party to the House.

Davis’s challenge is to retain voters who may have supported Trump while persuading them that he remains the right representative for their district.

4. Maine: An Open Seat Creates an Opportunity

Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is an important contest following Democratic Representative Jared Golden’s decision not to seek reelection.

Republican former Governor Paul LePage is challenging Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap for the seat. Trump carried the district by nine percentage points in 2024, giving Republicans a potentially favorable starting point.

The candidates’ financial positions have differed. LePage raised more than twice Dunlap’s reported fundraising total through June and held a substantial cash advantage. Democrats subsequently included Dunlap in their Red to Blue program, which identifies candidates the party is prioritizing in competitive races. 

Polling has offered a less straightforward picture than the district’s presidential voting history alone might suggest. Recent surveys cited in the original reporting showed a close contest, although polling sponsored by a candidate’s own party should be assessed with its methodology and potential limitations in mind.

The race will test whether Republicans can translate Trump’s strength in the district into a House victory or whether Democrats can retain the seat through a competitive open-seat campaign.

5. Ohio: Max Miller Faces Questions Over Allegations

Republican Representative Max Miller is seeking another term in a district he won by 15 percentage points in 2024. However, allegations of domestic and child abuse have brought additional scrutiny to his campaign.

Miller has denied the allegations. Republican Senator Bernie Moreno, whose daughter is Miller’s former wife, has called on the congressman to resign and withdraw from the race, according to the supplied reporting.

Democrat Brian Poindexter, an ironworker and Brook Park city councilor, is challenging Miller. Democrats have included Poindexter in their Red to Blue program and invested significantly in the contest. 

The race raises questions about whether controversy surrounding an incumbent can change the dynamics of a district that previously leaned Republican.

Campaign spending and party support will be important, but the allegations should be distinguished from established findings. Miller’s denial also remains relevant to how the claims are reported.

6. Iowa: Affordability Takes Center Stage

Democrat Christina Bohannan is challenging Republican Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks for the third consecutive election cycle, after losing to her in 2022 and 2024.

This year’s contest is unfolding amid concerns about the cost of living. Tariffs, fuel prices, and higher costs for agricultural inputs such as diesel and fertilizer have become part of the political debate.

The candidates had raised roughly comparable amounts through June, but Bohannan began July with a reported cash advantage of more than $730,000. Democrats had also outspent Republicans in the district by more than $3 million, according to the figures in the supplied report. 

For Iowa voters, the election offers a direct test of how economic pressures influence congressional contests. Farmers may be particularly attentive to fuel and fertilizer costs, while other households are focused on everyday expenses.

Bohannan’s repeated challenges make this a closely watched race, but her previous defeats underline why campaign spending and economic dissatisfaction do not guarantee an upset.

7. Florida: Maria Elvira Salazar Breaks With Trump on Immigration

Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar has publicly criticized aspects of Trump’s immigration policies, warning that some enforcement efforts have gone too far.

Her comments create a potential political tension. Salazar represents a South Florida district that Trump won by nearly 15 percentage points in 2024, but her criticism could appeal to voters who support tougher border controls while objecting to particular enforcement measures.

Her Democratic challenger, former television news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, has received support through the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s Red to Blue program. The supplied report described the race as competitive, with a poll showing Salazar narrowly ahead within the margin of error. 

The contest highlights the difficulty of balancing party loyalty with district-specific concerns. Immigration can be a powerful issue in Florida, but voters’ views are shaped by more than a single policy position.

Whether Salazar’s criticism of the administration helps her maintain a distinct political identity or creates friction with Republican voters remains a key question in the campaign.

8. Washington: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez Relies on a Cross-Party Appeal

Democratic Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez has sometimes broken with her party, including by supporting Republican positions on procedural votes and backing a resolution condemning another Democrat.

She faces Republican John Braun, the state Senate’s Republican leader, in a district that narrowly supported Trump in 2024.

Gluesenkamp Perez has reported a substantial fundraising advantage, although Republicans have spent more than Democrats in the district, according to the supplied figures. A September poll cited in the original report showed Braun leading by one percentage point. 

Her approach reflects a broader challenge for lawmakers representing politically divided districts: demonstrating independence without alienating their party’s core supporters.

The outcome could offer insight into whether a moderate or cross-party voting record helps an incumbent appeal to voters who split their choices between presidential and congressional candidates.

9. Kentucky: An Open Seat Gives Democrats a Target

Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District is competitive following Republican Representative Andy Barr’s decision to pursue his party’s nomination for the Senate.

Republican Ralph Alvarado, a former Kentucky state senator and former head of Tennessee’s health department, is running against Democrat Zach Dembo, a former Navy judge advocate general officer and federal prosecutor.

The candidates have raised similar amounts, and the parties have spent roughly comparable sums on the contest. The supplied report cited Democratic-sponsored polls showing Dembo ahead, despite Trump having carried the district by 15 percentage points in 2024. 

The race illustrates why an open seat can differ from a contest involving an incumbent. Without an established officeholder on the ballot, both parties have an opportunity to introduce their candidates to voters and define the central issues.

However, polling sponsored by one side does not establish that the district has shifted permanently toward the other party. The final outcome will depend on turnout, campaign performance, and the choices of voters who may have supported Trump in the presidential election.

10. California: Redistricting Produces Unusual Intra-Party Contests

California’s top-two primary system can produce general elections in which candidates from the same party face one another. The state’s redrawn congressional map has created unusual contests involving Republican Representatives Ken Calvert and Young Kim, according to the supplied report.

Democratic Representative Doris Matsui is also facing Sacramento City Council member Mai Vang, a democratic socialist.

Matsui has received support from prominent Democrats, including Governor Gavin Newsom, both of California’s US senators, and members of the state’s congressional delegation, as described in the original reporting.

These races differ from the other contests on this list because they do not necessarily determine which party controls the House. Instead, they could influence the makeup of a future Democratic majority or the ideological balance within a party.

The outcomes will help determine which candidates represent these districts, even if the overall partisan balance of the chamber remains unchanged.

What Issues Could Decide the 2026 Midterms?

Although the candidates and districts differ, several themes recur across the contests.

The economy and cost of living

Affordability is a central concern in Iowa and other competitive districts. Voters’ views on prices, energy costs, and economic policy could affect how they judge the party controlling Washington.

Immigration and Trump’s policies

Salazar’s criticism of immigration enforcement illustrates how the president’s policies can create different pressures for Republicans in different districts. Candidates must weigh national party priorities against the views of their own constituents.

Redistricting and electoral geography

Changes to district boundaries have altered the competitive landscape in states such as Texas and North Carolina. But redistricting is not a guarantee of victory, as the competitiveness of some newly drawn districts demonstrates.

Candidate controversies and personal credibility

Miller’s campaign in Ohio shows how allegations and political disputes can affect an incumbent’s reelection bid. Such claims must be reported with clear attribution and without presenting allegations as established facts.

Fundraising and campaign spending

Money helps campaigns reach voters through advertising, organizing, and other outreach. However, a financial advantage does not necessarily translate into votes, and reported totals can change as campaigns file updated disclosures.

When Are the 2026 US Midterm Elections?

Election Day is November 3, 2026. Voters will choose all 435 voting members of the House of Representatives, along with senators and numerous state and local officials.

The final outcome will depend on the combined results across districts rather than on any single headline contest. New York, Texas, North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Florida, Washington, Kentucky, and California each illustrate different aspects of the wider political battle.

The Bottom Line

The 2026 House elections will test the strength of the Republican majority and Democrats’ ability to turn national political dissatisfaction into victories in individual districts.

Republicans are using redistricting and campaign resources to defend their position, while Democrats are targeting vulnerable incumbents and open seats. Economic concerns, immigration policy, candidate controversies, and local political identities could all shape the results.

With Democrats needing a net gain of four seats, the outcome may hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races. Polls and fundraising reports provide clues about the campaigns, but neither can substitute for the votes cast on November 3.

news.title: How Trump’s disaster aid delays and FEMA cuts could galvanize the ‘movable middle’ in the 2026 elections
news.text:
When Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle on Oct. 9, 2026, it was just the latest weather disaster for Americans in a year that continues to break records.

The hottest U.S. summer on record left millions of Americans facing life-threatening heat waves. Extreme heat and drought set the stage for wildfires. Flooding from powerful storms and days of heavy rainfall inundated communities in several states. And now a “Super El Niño,” on top of already rising temperatures and sea levels, is expected to make extreme events worse, at least into spring 2027.

In the past, states relied heavily on federal aid and expertise to respond quickly to disasters. But in communities across the U.S., people recovering from floods, storms and wildfires in 2025 and 2026 have been left waiting much longer for federal aid – if it arrives at all.

Will there be political consequences in the midterm elections for the slow aid and lack of government assistance?

The answer to that question runs through the ways the Trump administration has changed disaster response and federal disaster aid. As a professor who has written for years about civic engagement and climate policy, I have reason to believe that voters’ frustration with slow disaster aid may show up at the polls.

Cuts to FEMA hobbled federal disaster help

Even though the United States is experiencing more disasters as the climate changes, the federal programs meant to help Americans recover are being diminished.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has faced significant cuts to funding and staff since the Trump administration took office in January 2025. The administration initially talked about abolishing the agency, arguing that states and communities could deal with disasters on their own. It created a plan to cut FEMA’s staffing by 50%, but in September 2026, a judge found that plan to be unlawful.

FEMA lost over 17% of its trained staff members in 2025 alone, including hundreds of people who were on call to respond to disasters. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to defend the administration’s goal of a leaner workforce at the agency.

The Trump administration also withheld billions of dollars meant to help states reduce their disaster risk and protect homes, hospitals and other structures from storm damage. Lawsuits forced the administration to restore some of the funds, but many communities are still struggling on their own.

These changes have tangible effects on how well states are able to recover from disasters and how well they can prepare for the disaster risks ahead as the climate changes.

Slower aid, if it arrives at all

The Trump administration is also taking longer to approve emergency funding after disasters than past administrations did and denying more of those requests.

In 2025 it denied 26% of requests for major disaster declarations, which unlock immediate federal aid. That was up from an average of 15% over the previous two decades.

An independent analysis of FEMA data exposes some clear patterns in funding delays under the Trump administration. The review found that major disaster declarations have taken an average of nearly 10 weeks to be issued during the current Trump administration, up from an average of three weeks or less over the previous two decades.

The administration says it is simply conducting more thorough reviews when governors make these aid requests. But people caught in disasters don’t have time to wait. Major disaster aid includes individual assistance, such as temporary housing, loans and repair grants, that disaster survivors need quickly to recover.

The review also found that about 85% of the requests for federal assistance from states that went for Donald Trump in the 2024 election were eventually approved, while only about half of requests have been approved in states that voted for his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris. 

A separate Associated Press report in July 2026 noted that no other president had such a sharp partisan divide in approving disaster declaration requests between Republican and Democratic governors since at least 1989, when a federal law set rules for disaster determinations.

Disaster failures can mobilize political moderates

A handful of studies, including mine, have found that people who have experienced a disaster often have higher levels of civic engagement.

In my study, civic engagement included contacting elected officials, signing petitions, attending public meetings, participating in boycotts or joining protests, among other actions. We didn’t look at the connection to voting patterns, but I believe there is good reason to expect our findings to extend to voting as well.

The relationship between experiencing a disaster and level of civic engagement was strongest for political moderates who are sometimes referred to as the “movable middle” – they could swing in either political direction if they have reason to do so.

Given the disasters America has seen in recent years and the sharp drop in federal assistance, I expect that political moderates who become more civically engaged will play a significant role in the midterm elections this year.

How FEMA cuts play out in a crisis

Several recent disasters have shown what happens when the federal government isn’t prepared to respond quickly.

After the devastating July 4 floods that swept through Texas Hill Country in 2025, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees FEMA, waited three days before approving funding to send federal search-and-rescue teams, a Congressional report confirmed. Other funding approvals took an average of 12 days, leaving local and state programs to fill critical gaps in disaster systems.

In summer 2026, Texas was hit with floods again. The president approved assistance for some of the counties after a seven-week delay. Other requests for assistance were still waiting months later.

FEMA denied individual and statewide assistance to Michigan after severe storms and tornadoes tore up homes across several rural communities in March 2026.

With highly contested Senate races looming in both states, these actions by the Trump administration could color voters’ views or contribute to a lack of enthusiasm for the party in power and even increase support for the opposition.

A survey conducted by Pew Research Center in May 2025 found that the majority of Americans believe that it is a good idea for the federal government to provide financial assistance to help people rebuild after disasters in place at high risk of extreme weather. 

These findings are relatively consistent across political parties: 60% of those who identified as Republican or leaning Republican said they believed it was a good idea, as did 68% of those who identified as Democrat or leaning Democrat.

Too little, too late?

Trump recently started announcing disaster aid approvals in states consequential to the control of Congress in the midterm elections, including in Wisconsin and Ohio. In some cases, he coupled his candidate endorsements with disaster funding announcements. 

I don’t believe those late announcements will move the needle in his party’s favor at this late date.

news.title: Democrats slam Iran war gas prices but keep their climate surcharges
news.text:
Just in time for election season, climate leftists have discovered the price of gasoline. On cable news, in Congress, and across social media, Democrats are eager to remind drivers what they're paying at the pump. Their outrage stops where their climate agenda begins.

On October 5, the national average for regular gasoline stood near $4.37, according to AAA, after the most expensive September on record. Compare state averages by the governor's party, and Democrats have a problem.

The real existential threat was never at the pump. It's sitting in Tehran. Voters should remember which threat leftists actually treated like one.

Across the 26 Republican-governed states, regular gas averaged about $4.24 a gallon. Across the 24 Democrat-governed states, it averaged $4.53 — nearly 7% more. Diesel showed a similar gap: about $6.15 versus $6.50. Those are unweighted averages of state prices, not the entire explanation for the difference. But state policy adds to the bill.

The cost of climate policy

California, Washington, and Oregon have all placed transportation fuels under climate programs with costs that can reach motorists.

California's cap-and-trade program and Low Carbon Fuel Standard added about 42 cents per gallon in January 2026, according to the state’s Energy Commission. Washington’s Climate Commitment Act requires covered fuel suppliers to buy emissions allowances. Oregon’s Climate Protection Program caps emissions from fossil fuels, including gasoline and diesel.

These policies don’t account for every cent at the pump. Refining constraints, geography, and global crude prices count too. But Democratic officials chose to make fossil fuels more expensive to advance their climate goals.

The early October prices tell the story: California, $6.38 a gallon; Washington, $5.48; Oregon, $5.04. Those Democrat-run states enforce climate mandates on top of ordinary fuel taxes. Their leaders should answer for the costs they have chosen to impose.

We've heard this before

In June 2022, the national average for regular gas reached a record $5.01 a gallon. What answer did Americans hear from Democratic leaders as prices climbed? Buy an electric vehicle.

In November 2021, President Joe Biden said EV owners could save $800 to $1,000 in fuel costs that year. He had recently test-driven an electric Hummer priced above $112,000. In March 2022, Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg joined Vice President Kamala Harris to promote electric transportation and the administration's $5 billion charging network. That June, then-Senator Debbie Stabenow (D-Mich.) told a Senate hearing that she had driven her EV from Michigan to Washington, passing gas stations where the price no longer mattered to her.

For families who couldn't afford a new electric car, the advice offered little relief. The administration presented electrification as its answer to expensive gasoline. Climate policy had its price, and drivers were expected to accept it.

RELATED: One atmosphere, 50 courts — what could go wrong?

 Megane Adam/Getty Images

A threat beyond the gas pump

Then came October 7, 2023. Iran-backed Hamas terrorists crossed into Israel and murdered about 1,200 people in the deadliest attack on Jews since the Holocaust. The danger came from armed men serving a terrorist organization supported by Tehran, not from a projected rise in sea levels.

Iran's nuclear ambitions remain largely unchecked. Before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on its enrichment facilities, Tehran had enriched uranium to 60% purity, close to weapons-grade. It has since refused international inspectors access to bombed sites and failed to account fully for its stockpile. The status of its enrichment capacity remains uncertain, but it's no longer a hypothetical threat decades away.

The war with Iran has also helped drive oil and gasoline prices higher. Climate Democrats now want credit for noticing the cost. Fine. They should explain why raising fuel costs to meet climate targets is defensible but paying more to confront a regime that arms terrorist proxies and refuses to account for highly enriched uranium is beyond the pale.

The real existential threat was never at the pump. It's sitting in Tehran. Voters should remember which threat leftists actually treated like one.

news.title: Susan Collins, Troy Jackson in a coin toss, Maine Senate poll finds
news.text:
The crucial Senate race in Maine is a coin-toss, a new Suffolk University Poll finds, with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson at 49% and Republican incumbent Susan Collins at 47%.

At stake in the contest could be control of the Senate.

As Democratic candidates surge in competitive Senate races across the country, Collins has managed to stay all but tied by holding a narrow edge among independent voters and even drawing a 14% slice of those who disapprove of President Donald Trump.

The survey of 500 likely voters, taken by landline and cellphone Oct. 8-11, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points.

"Either through her seniority as senator, her branding as a moderate, or possibly from disgruntled Graham Platner voters who were forced to relinquish his Democratic Party nomination, somehow Collins is starting to erode the Democratic base of Jackson just enough to keep the race close," said David Paleologos, director of Suffolk University's Political Research Center. "As of today, the race hasn't broken open."

Platner withdrew from the campaign in July after a former girlfriend accused him of rape and sexual abuse. He has denied the allegations.

Gains among independent voters have boosted Democratic Senate nominees Josh Turek in Iowa and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, both key races, in recent Suffolk surveys.

To win control, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats and hold all the Democratic ones.

In Maine's campaign, Collins has emphasized her independence from Trump, while Democrats have sought to tie her to the president, including her critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Bret Kavanaugh.

Looking at crossovers: Collins has gotten support from 5% of the voters who reported backing Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race. That's more than the support Jackson gets from just one of the 237 respondents who said they had backed Trump.

A vote against the times, not for a candidate

The poll found a pessimistic public, disgruntled by the nation's politics.

The most frequent motivation cited for voting in the midterms was "expressing dissatisfaction with the current national political climate," followed closely by "fulfilling my civic duty." Only one in 10 said they were voting to support a specific candidate's vision.

Trump's disapproval-approval rating was a dismal 57%-37%. Even more, 64%, said the country was "on the wrong track."

Nearly 6 in 10, 58%, rated economic conditions in Maine as "poor." Only 7% said they were excellent or good.

The cost of gas and fuel prices topped the list of economic issues impacting their household budgets, cited by 36%. That was nearly double the No. 2 issue, grocery costs.

Worries about a cold winter

Heating oil is a particularly powerful issue in Maine, where about two-thirds of households use petroleum products to heat their homes, the highest of any state. As winter approaches, disruptions from the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine conflict have contributed to fuel prices that have neared record highs.

In the governor's race, Democrat Hannah Pingree led Republican Robert Charles by double digits, 49%-38%. Independent Rick Bennett was backed by 8%, with 5% undecided. Term limits prevented the Democratic incumbent, Janet Mills, from seeking a third term.

The two Senate candidates met the night of Oct. 13 in the third of four scheduled debates.

Susan Page, the Washington Bureau chief of USA TODAY, has covered the past 12 presidential elections.

news.title: Kamala Harris fuels 2028 White House speculation with campaign blitz across key states
news.text:
Kamala Harris is expanding her late-fall campaign tour in support of Democratic candidates, setting up a travel plan that will take her across several key 2028 early primary states before Election Day as the former vice president weighs a potential future run for the White House.

Running from Oct. 21 through Oct. 30, the widened final leg of her itinerary adds stops in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, and Mississippi, as well as a digital appearance in Florida, per details provided by her office. These join previously scheduled visits to Nevada and Georgia.

Though Harris has repeatedly stated in recent media appearances that her immediate focus is securing Democratic victories this autumn, she has left open the possibility of another bid for the presidency following her 2024 defeat to Donald Trump.

The late-October travel focuses heavily on candidates seeking office as governor or in the U.S. Senate, creating opportunities for the first Black woman to hold the office of vice president to rally with contenders who could also make history.

The tour begins Oct. 21 in Nevada alongside Aaron Ford, the state's first Black attorney general, who is bidding to become its first Black governor, along with additional Democratic nominees. 

She is also slated to meet members of the Culinary Workers Union in the state, which hosts the second nominating primary on the 2028 Democratic calendar behind South Carolina.

On Oct. 22, Harris travels to Mississippi to campaign with Scott Colom, who is vying to become the state's first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era. Colom's bid against incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has increasingly drawn national Democratic interest.

Moving on to New Hampshire on Oct. 24, Harris will join Senate nominee Chris Pappas for an event focused on reproductive healthcare and abortion access. 

During her tenure as vice president, she served as the primary voice for abortion rights within the Biden administration, particularly during the 2022 midterms. New Hampshire is slated third in the 2028 nominating process.

She will then appear in Wisconsin alongside gubernatorial nominee David Crowley on Oct. 26, before embarking on a three-day tour of Georgia starting Oct. 28. Her Georgia schedule includes appearances with Sen. Jon Ossoff, voter protection gatherings, and an address at the Fulton County Democratic Party's annual gala in Atlanta on Oct. 30.

During her time in Georgia, Harris will lead an online organizing session for Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon, who aims to become Florida's first Black U.S. senator. 

The joint event connects Harris, a figure rooted in mainstream establishment politics, with a prominent progressive candidate. Nixon, a state legislator who identifies as a democratic socialist, commands backing among left-wing supporters who previously viewed Harris as overly moderate in 2024.

This final swing builds upon earlier virtual and physical events, fundraising efforts, and voting rights initiatives supported by Harris, including work with the Democratic National Committee. 

Her most recent outreach included a trip to Michigan to support another high-profile progressive, Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and deliver remarks at an NAACP event.

news.title: You bailed on TV. But politicians are still spending all their money there.
news.text: If you ask pundits, 2024 was the Podcast Election (which also means it was the YouTube Election). And maybe 2026 is the Influencer Election. One thing the chattering class won't call it is the Television Election — because everyone knows everyone has stopped watching TV. Except that's not how political campaigns are run, at all. Even in 2026, more than 60% of the estimated $11.6 billion spent in this election cycle will go to good ol' fashioned broadcast and cable TV. Another 20% will be spent on streaming TV. If you think that doesn't leave a lot of room for things where you and most people you know spend a ton of time — YouTube, Reels, TikTok, etc. — you're right. Political pros know it, too. So why isn't that changing? I asked Rob Flaherty, who has spent most of his life doing digital politics for Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and, most recently, Kamala Harris. Flaherty offered up a bunch of reasons why TV remains so dominant in political spending, even as it gets less relevant to voters. But a base reason is simply that political operatives spent money on TV because other political operatives spend money there: Flaherty even admits that in his current work — co-running an anti-AI super PAC — he has been buying some TV time just so other people in politics will take him seriously. You can hear our entire conversation about how campaigns work in the TikTok era — and how they ought to work — on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our chat. Peter Kafka: You said that when you were working on the Harris campaign, you spent roughly 50-50 between TV and digital — but that most campaigns still spend 70% of their budget on TV. Make the best case for why a campaign should still spend half or more of its money on TV. Rob Flaherty: Well, I would not advocate for that. But I think the steelman case that you would hear is: Digital political ad inventory is actually quite limited. There are only so many places you can spend. Social media is not a mind-changing surface; it's a base-building surface. Meanwhile, television is concentrating on a smaller number of higher-view surfaces. So you actually want to spend more money on TV because it's more expensive to buy against an NFL game than it was just to buy across from the local news and in prime time. That sounds a lot like the TV industry's own argument for years: "Yes, ratings are down, but that means the shows people are still watching are more valuable." Look, this is an industry that has a nobody-ever-got-fired-for-hiring-McKinsey problem. If you do the same thing everyone else does and you lose, then you did everything right. And if you try something different and you lose, it's you who made bad decisions. I'll even say candidly: I run Tomorrow Together, a new super PAC where we just launched a bunch of ads. We're advertising against people who don't want AI regulations. And even I — Mr. F—ing Digital — felt this pull, like I needed to have pretty significant TV spending. Because otherwise the industry won't view it as legit, because TV is legit. We still spent mostly on digital, largely because it's a super PAC and we're spending late. But I prioritized making sure we had some TV in there, because otherwise people don't think it's real. And also, the way a lot of this works is: The general consultants who are the top consultants to the candidate, very often are economically tied to the margins of TV. Spell that out. You're running a campaign. Why do you have an economic incentive to buy TV? Because you get a cut of the buy. The more TV a campaign buys, the more money you make. Basically. Usually, the general consultant hires up all the other consultants. Those consultants get a cut, either a fee or a cut of media spend. TV margins are great. They are really, really great. They are better than digital margins. For the consultant, you're making 10%, 15% on a TV buy. And by "margins," you mean the money the person buying the ads gets from the campaign? Yeah. You make more money because there's just less staff time. The other thing that's crazy is a lot of the big TV firms don't actually do the buying. They subcontract to one of three or four buying shops. So everybody's just making money all over the place. There's a rent-seeking thing: The most senior consultants who have been around for a while came up in TV. They talk to the candidates. They push them to spend more on TV. And then you have campaign managers who are typically relatively more junior, particularly on Senate races, who don't want to mess up. They don't want to do something different and radical, and they have to convince the candidate and the general consultant anyway. So you end up in this place where the easiest thing to do is just sort of the same thing. The broader media business had the same problem: Advertisers took a long time to follow consumers to digital. They were still spending on TV when people were leaving in droves. Does politics eventually catch up? If you talk to any politician, they would tell you digital is very important. It's the internet. And then you look at their media mix, and it's not that. I do think presidential primaries are what drive innovation in politics. I do think you're going to see some people try a bunch of new stuff, and then that will lead to a more cogent theory of how you spend more of your campaign dollars on the places where people actually are. I'm hopeful that change is coming. But so much of the way that media gets spent is profit-seeking and rent-seeking that you do have to break through that. It has the entrenched layer of political power on top of it, and that is one of the reasons.
news.summary: Audiences have been leaving TV for the internet for a very long time. Most advertisers have figured that out some time ago. But not political ones.

news.title: Democrats' not-so-secret midterm campaigns for the White House
news.text:
They're off, already.

While the midterms are officially about electing 36 governors and 470 members of Congress, a burgeoning group of prominent and wannabe prominent Democrats are using this political season to pursue a higher aspiration: The 2028 presidential nomination.

The days when political protocol required early White House hopefuls to be coy?

"I'm thinking about it," said former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party's late-breaking nominee in 2024. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg acknowledged that he's "more inclined than not" to run. Asked by USA TODAY to name a reason he might not run, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear cited only objections from his family − then noted that his wife and two children had always supported his campaigns.

More: New 2028 presidential poll shows 2 potential frontrunners

The GOP has a presumptive 2028 nominee in Vice President JD Vance, although he is likely to face challengers. (Vance's prediction to NBC: "It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, [Texas Sen.] Ted Cruz is running for president.")

But Democrats are heading toward a big roster and a fierce battle over the 2028 nomination. While Harris leads early polls, no dominant frontrunner defines the race. The field is wide open and so is the direction of the party amid a rising debate between advocates in the middle and those on the left.

Consider the lanes: The governors, with seven or so regularly mentioned. The senators, with at least nine early prospects. The progressives, including New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Rep. Ro Khanna. A handful of formers who are out of government and want back in, among them Rahm Emanuel, who is not only a former Chicago mayor and House member but also a former ambassador and White House chief of staff.

Here are five ways they and others are pursuing the White House now.

More: Kamala Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and the rocky midterms campaign trail

Like the guy in the Johnny Cash song, Pete Buttigieg has been everywhere.

In the two years since he lost his job as transportation secretary with President Donald Trump's inauguration, Buttigieg has visited 37 states, Politico first calculated, and campaigned in person for about half of the 100 candidates he has endorsed. In the final weeks before the midterms, spokesman Sean Manning says his travel schedule includes at least six states, including Michigan and Virginia, which hold early 2028 primaries.

Buttigieg signals his ambitions with the name of his political action committee: Win the Era.

Buttigieg, a former mayor of South Bend, Indiana, has made several stops in South Carolina, which has been designated by the Democratic National Committee as the first presidential primary.

That helps explain why New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Beshear, Emanuel and Khanna have also had South Carolina on their itineraries this fall.

Not to mention Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly. He spent the Oct. 9-11 weekend on a swing through Michigan with his wife, former congresswoman Gabby Giffords. During the midterms, he's been on the road, too. To more than 15 states. So far.

Send a check

Sending a check to a campaign or holding a fundraiser for a candidate is a way to make connections and gather chits.

Kamala Harris has headlined fundraisers for Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, among others, and she's scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the annual Fulton County Democratic Party fundraiser on Oct. 30 in Atlanta.

When Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa was gaining ground in her challenge to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, she had just $4 million in the bank, according to Texas campaign records. The Democratic Governors Association − whose chairman happens to be Beshear − and Pritzker each dispatched $1 million to help.

Pritzker, a billionaire heir to the Hyatt Hotels fortune, has been particularly generous, dispensing tens of millions of dollars during this cycle outside his home state of Illinois. He has contributed to the House Majority PAC, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and to Senate nominees Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Jon Ossoff in Georgia, among others.

Because money talks.

In the contest to criticize President Donald Trump − a risk-free enterprise for Democrats − Newsom has taken the early lead.

"The gravest threat to American democracy," Newsom said of Trump, warning Americans, "Wake up: You will lose your country." He called the president "corrupt and unstable" and his deployment of National Guard troops to Los Angeles a "brazen abuse of power."

Then there was Trump's comment Oct. 5 at a Nebraska rally, discussing the Iran war: "They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." (The White House later said the president meant that the cities were vulnerable to an attack, not that he was inviting one.)

"He is deranged and dangerous," Newsom said in response. He directed California's State Threat Assessment Center "to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President's remarks as an invitation to target California."

Bash fellow Democrats

That's an even more reliable way to get attention: Scold fellow Democrats.

Newsom has criticized some Democrats for not doing more to confront Republicans.

Pritzker has accused some Democrats of lacking the backbone to counter GOP attacks on hot-button issues like transgender rights. "Those same do-nothing Democrats want to blame our losses on our defense of Black people, of trans kids, of immigrants, instead of their own lack of guts and gumption."

And Emanuel has put a critique of the Democratic Party at the center of his message.

"We've lost the plot because the party got un-anchored," he told a Fox News podcast, by focusing on the culture wars instead of the concerns of middle-class voters about the economy and education. "You are worried about bathroom access and locker room access," he said. "Why don't you focus on classroom excellence?"

Blasting what he calls the party's "leftward lurch," he labels himself a "raging moderate."

To win in 2028? Try someone like, well, me

Emanuel says a raging moderate could succeed in winning back the White House in 2028 − that is, someone like him. He's released a series of policy proposals, including restricting children's access to social media and banning federal workers from betting on the predictions market.

AOC says contenders in the midterms like Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed are proving that voices advocating significant progressive change − say, someone like her − can energize new voters and reinvigorate the party. "We have written a check on the left, saying if you champion these policies that have popular support, we can win," she said in remarks at a New York fundraiser leaked to ABC. "And now it is time to cash in."

Beshear argues the presidential appeal of governors who have records of solving problems and reaching across partisan lines. "I believe that our candidate should be a Democratic governor, and there's lots of Democratic governors that appear to be looking at this, and there's lots of great ones," he told USA TODAY.

Someone like him?

Susan Page, the Washington Bureau chief of USA TODAY, has covered the past 12 presidential elections.

news.title: At Least It's Just the Plague
news.text: I’m a millennial, just about. That means that, so far, I’ve lived through the threat of nuclear annihilation, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the genocides of the 1990s, the horror of 9/11, the financial crisis of 2008 and, of course, the coronavirus pandemic. To paraphrase Donald Rumsfeld, “stuff happened,” and while objectively the world is in a far better place now than in the early 1980s, I think this has likely contributed to my fatalistic view of life. The reason I raise this isn’t to solicit an outbreak of correspondence therapy. It’s in response to an email from Newsweek member Raymond Waller, who also identifies as an “elder millennial” and reacted to our report about the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia. “At least it’s just the plague,” he wrote. He explained that it was necessary to establish whether it was untreatable or some novel variant before calibrating a response. Quite right (and I mean that sincerely). Let’s not overreact to murky indications of a potential pestilential apocalypse when the president is too unstable to remain in office. Yes, that brings us to the other Donald, again. Following Trump’s endorsement of an Iranian attack on Los Angeles and San Diego, California Governor Gavin Newsom and other Democrats demanded that his Cabinet invoke the 25th Amendment. That report triggered a verdict on our Fairness Meter, and 31 percent of readers rated the article right-leaning. Our report about the Russian plague case, meanwhile, was rated left-leaning by 13 percent of readers, with not a single vote for right-wing bias. I’m not sure what to make of this. Democrats want the president removed, and even reporting this as a partisan demand with a White House response is seen to favor Republicans, but, at the same time, the Black Death has apparently joined the Democratic Party. There is a virus spreading through America, but it’s not the Russian plague, Yersinia pestis. It’s Partisanus hystericus: Highly contagious, particularly in Washington, and resistant to reason. The 25th Amendment is an interesting mechanism for removing a president. It was designed to address inability, not provide an ejector seat whenever the opposition finds a president’s remarks objectionable. That hasn’t stopped Democrats demanding its use against Trump. Nor did it stop Republicans demanding the same remedy against Joe Biden, particularly after his disastrous 2024 debate performance. Republican Representative Chip Roy introduced a resolution urging Vice President Kamala Harris to invoke the amendment, and House Speaker Mike Johnson said the Cabinet should discuss it. When Biden abandoned his reelection campaign the following month, Missouri Senator Eric Schmitt wrote to Cabinet secretaries demanding his removal. His reasoning was that a man incapable of running for president was incapable of being president. Presumably that disqualifies the vast majority of Americans. Now the parties have swapped places, but the constitutional diagnosis remains the same. If everything a president does or says is treated as a five-alarm fire, we can’t calibrate a response. Let’s take Raymond Waller’s advice: slow down, assess and let nature (or elections) take their course before reaching for that ejector seat.

By Associated Press

WASHINGTON: Vice President Kamala Harris tested positive for COVID-19 on Tuesday, the White House announced, underscoring the persistence of the highly contagious virus even as the U.S. eases restrictions in a bid to return to pre-pandemic normalcy.

Neither President Joe Biden nor first lady Jill Biden was considered a “close contact” of Harris in recent days, said the vice president’s press secretary, Kirsten Allen. Harris had been scheduled to attend Biden’s Tuesday morning Presidential Daily Brief but was not present, the White House said.

She had returned Monday from a weeklong trip to the West Coast. The last time she saw Biden was the previous Monday, April 18.

“I have no symptoms, and I will continue to isolate and follow CDC guidelines,” Harris tweeted. “I’m grateful to be both vaccinated and boosted.”

After consulting with her physicians, Harris, 57, was prescribed and is taking Paxlovid, the Pfizer antiviral pill, her office said late Tuesday. The drug, when administered within five days of symptoms appearing, has been proven to bring about a 90% reduction in hospitalizations and deaths among patients most likely to get severe disease.

Biden phoned Harris Tuesday afternoon to make sure she “has everything she needs” while working from home, the White House said.

Harris, received her first dose of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine weeks before taking office and a second dose just days after Inauguration Day in 2021. She received a booster shot in late October and an additional booster on April 1. Fully vaccinated and boosted people have a high degree of protection against serious illness and death from COVID-19, particularly from the most common and highly transmissible omicron variant.

Harris’ diagnosis comes a month after her husband, Doug Emhoff, recovered from the virus, as a wave of cases of the highly transmissible omicron subvariant has spread through Washington’s political class, infecting Cabinet members, White House staffers and lawmakers including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Chris Murphy, D-Conn., tested positive on Tuesday.

Allen said Harris would follow Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines “and the advice of her physicians.” It was not immediately clear whether she is being prescribed any antiviral treatments.

The White House has put in place strict COVID-19 protocols around the president, vice president and their spouses, including daily testing for those expected to be in close contact with them. Biden is tested regularly on the advice of his physician, the White House has said, and last tested negative on Monday.

“We have a very very contagious variant out there,” said White House COVID-19 coordinator Dr. Aashish Jha on Tuesday. “It is going to be hard to ensure that no one gets COVID in America. That’s not even a policy goal.” He said the administration’s goal is to make sure people don’t get seriously ill.

Jha added that despite the precautions it is possible that Biden himself will come down with the virus at some point.

“I wouldn’t say it’s just a matter of time, but of course it is possible that the president, like any other American, could get COVID,” he said. “There is no 100% anything.”

Psaki said she “would not expect” any changes to White House protocols.

After more than two years and nearly a million deaths in the U.S., the virus is still killing more than 300 people a day in the U.S., according to the CDC. The unvaccinated are at a far greater risk, more than twice as likely to test positive and nine times as likely to die from the virus as those who have received at least a primary dose of the vaccines, according to the public health agency.

Harris’ diagnosis comes as the Biden administration is taking steps to expand availability of the life-saving Paxlovid, reassuring doctors that there is ample supply for people at high risk of severe illness or death from the virus.

In addition to her husband’s diagnosis, Harris was identified as a “close contact” after her communications director tested positive on April 6.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention defines “close contact” with an infected person as spending 15 minutes or more with them over a 24-hour period. The CDC says people with “close contact” do not need to quarantine if they are up to date on their vaccines but should wear well-fitting masks around other people for 10 days after the contact.

news.title: Kamala Harris faces Democratic doubts over 2028 as allies push back on claims she’s squandered her chance
news.text: As former Vice President Kamala Harris weighs another White House run in 2028, a longtime advisor is firing back at Democratic strategists and donors who argue she has squandered an opportunity to politically reinvent herself following her 2024 election defeat. Veteran Democratic strategist Maria Cardona, an outside advisor to Harris, pushed back against the criticism highlighted in a new Politico report, defending Harris' policy proposals and campaign activity as Democrats debate whether the former vice president deserves another shot at the White House. Cardona argued the story was "infuriating in its silliness." The report, based on interviews with nearly 20 California-based Democratic donors and strategists, highlighted growing skepticism among some party insiders about Harris' political future and whether she has done enough to distinguish herself from her unsuccessful 2024 campaign. Longtime Democratic strategist Doug Herman, a veteran of former President Barack Obama’s 2008 and 2012 campaigns, told Politico that Harris "totally blew it... She hasn’t gotten into the mix." AOC GIVES MAJOR HINT ABOUT 2028 Former Gov. Jim Hodges of South Carolina, the lead off state in the Democratic Party's 2028 presidential nominating calendar, told Politico, "I don’t see anything different myself. It seems like more of the same to me." But Cardona, a veteran of the Bill Clinton administration, the Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama presidential campaigns who currently serves as a member of the Democratic National Committee, disagreed that Harris had failed to spell out what she would offer Democrats anxious for change. "How can you state that she hasn’t done anything new or groundbreaking or talked about new initiatives or policies and then layout exactly those policies - like proposing an expanded Supreme Court, lowering the voting age to 16, making DC and Puerto Rico states. Those are pretty groundbreaking policies!" Cardona told Fox News Digital, as she pointed to some of Harris' moves since the end of former President Joe Biden's administration. Harris, the nation's first Black vice president, has also said that Black people should be "transactional voters," instead of automatically supporting Democratic candidates. "She’s damned if she does and damned if she doesn’t," Cardona argued, adding that Harris "is still the most qualified person to be president of the United States that is mentioned as a possible candidate for 2028." Harris has been crisscrossing the country this year, first on a book tour for her best-selling campaign memoir "107 Days" and currently to support fellow Democrats running in the midterm elections. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB While Harris has teamed up with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and congressional nominees in her home state, some Democratic nominees running in red states made headlines in recent weeks by asking the former vice president not to campaign with them. But Cardona said, "Harris has been out there nonstop talking to young voters, women voters, black voters, Latino voters, and she has been asked by many candidates to come and campaign with them. She has focused her energies on winning the midterm elections. Can you imagine the backlash if she was out there focusing on herself and how she can remake the Democratic Party?" Harris replaced Biden as the Democrats' 2024 presidential nominee after he ended his re-election bid following a disastrous debate performance against President Donald Trump. Her truncated three-month presidential campaign ended in defeat, with Trump narrowly sweeping all the key battleground states as he won back the White House. If she runs a third time for president, Harris will enjoy instant name ID and plenty of goodwill from within her party. But she would also face a Democratic base trying to move past the 2024 election setbacks, and she would likely be part of a very crowded and competitive 2028 primary field. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER A Democratic consultant, who asked for anonymity to speak more freely, told Fox News Digital that "voters feel like they haven't heard much from Harris, which means bad memories from her 2024 election loss remain fresh in their minds." But longtime Democratic strategist Michael Ceraso said that consultants "are not voters." "I just don’t trust that the consulting class really has a finger on the electorate," he told Fox News Digital. "To listen to consultants saying Harris has blown it – presidential politics hasn’t really even started yet.. These consultants are just getting soundbites." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ceraso noted that it took Biden three runs to win the White House. "The third time was the charm and everybody said to Biden when he ran the third time, ‘why are you running.’ Well guess what, he ended up becoming the nominee and the president," he said. "Why can’t Harris look at that template and say ‘that can apply to me too.’"

news.title: Kamala Harris warns window closing for AI safeguards, urges US-China cooperation
news.text:
SEOUL: Former US Vice President Kamala Harris urged governments and technology companies on Wednesday to urgently put safeguards in place for artificial intelligence, warning that the window for containing its gravest risks was closing.

“If we are to have any guardrails and safeguards, they have to be at the table,” Harris said of AI developers during an appearance at South Korea’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies.

“My concern is that the window is shutting.”

Harris said governments and companies must act immediately against what she described as three existential dangers from AI - cybersecurity threats, AI-enabled weapons and systems escaping human control.

She also urged the United States to engage China on international rules and standards for AI, saying their broader strategic rivalry should not preclude cooperation on shared risks.

“There is room for cooperation where our interests are aligned,” Harris said, calling for “healthy and robust competition, but not conflict.”

Harris criticised what she called US President Donald Trump’s “erratic tariffs” and their punitive nature, before warning against a transactional approach that cost the US global influence.

“The question is, are we thinking only about the short term, or do we also value and appreciate the significance of an investment for long-term gain?” Harris praised South Korean investment in US shipbuilding, semiconductors, electric vehicles and clean energy, calling it “immensely significant and valued”.

She also called for renewed US commitment to South Korea, saying growing cooperation among North Korea, Russia, China and Iran was very concerning and meant the allies must strengthen deterrence.

The former vice president has been campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections as she weighs another White House bid.

She said Democrats would win a majority in the House of Representatives and had a “very good shot” at taking the Senate, potentially giving Congress a stronger voice on domestic and foreign policy, including the war with Iran.

Asked whether she would again seek the presidency in 2028, Harris said: “I’m still thinking about it. I haven’t decided yet.”

news.title: Meet the youngest generation of Trump voters now turning their backs on Maga
news.text:
Welcome to Trump’s America, The i Paper’s World Insight series presenting the sharpest, deepest thinking on an era-defining shift in history and politics, investigating how Donald Trump and his administration have changed the US and the world – and where we go from here.

• We’ve reached “peak America” – just don’t tell Donald Trump• Brash America is facing its worst nightmare: loneliness• Maga’s worst nightmare: a child-free, unmarried female president

Kameron Zeka is annoyed with himself for voting for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. The 22-year-old, from a small town near Storm Lake in Iowa, is one of many Gen Z voters who backed the President but have now turned against him.

The fracturing of Trump’s coalition threatens to doom the Republican Party in the midterm elections next month, when Democrats are expected to take back the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.

Zeka, who works as a fertiliser drafter, knew that Trump was a wrecking ball when he voted for him but he thought was exactly what the country needed. “Our political system is so broken,” he tells The i Paper. At the time, he felt “we need somebody to come in and break it to the point where it actually is going to get repaired”.

“I thought Trump might get us to the point where Americans wake up and say, we have to take back our political system from these corporations,” he adds. 

“It seemed everything was fairly normal when Trump was President the first time … it wasn’t too crazy.”

He brushed off concerns from many of his friends, who are Mexican, that Trump would deport them and ignored his mother, who said that Trump was a fascist. And he agreed with some of the things that Trump was saying, including that Nato countries should pay more and there should be no new wars.

Looking back, he thinks: “It’s stupid to believe what I did.” 

Zeka’s regrets began within months. He was deeply upset with the President’s handling of the Epstein files. He was angry that the famous men who knew Jeffrey Epstein got away without being put on trial, especially as Trump was named in the documents. But when the war on Iran began on 28 February, Zeka finally lost faith in Trump. 

“It just seemed so dumb,” Zeka said. “Middle Eastern wars are a touchy subject for Americans. Trump says this one was for nuclear weapons, but a bunch of countries have nukes. North Korea has them and we haven’t been killed by them”.

Zeka is not alone. According to a recent poll by The New York Times, Trump’s approval rating among voters under 30 stands at a miserable 18 per cent. That is down 20 points from the 39 per cent of Gen Z who backed the President in the 2024 election. Trump came into office promising to end foreign wars and bring down grocery prices on day one. Instead he invaded Iran and gasoline is at its highest level in decades. For younger voters who cast their ballot in their first presidential election in 2024, the past few years have proved a brutal lesson in the realities of national politics.

“When I was at school I read the [Erik Larson] book In The Garden of the Beasts, about a US diplomat and his family who lived in Weimar Germany,” Zeka says. “It does seem every day like we’re getting closer and closer to something similar to that. I’m worried.”

The company where Zeka works is now “really struggling” due to the high cost of fertiliser. Some staff have had their hours cut from 45 to 40 a week and he fears his may be cut, too. He says he is paying hundreds of dollars more on groceries and fuel, with the cost rising with every week that passes. “I’m just disappointed with Trump,” Zeka says. “I think he’s a horrible person and I’m not happy with him.”

If Kamala Harris had taken over from Joe Biden, he believes, it “wouldn’t have been this bad”.

Addy Leugers, 21, was drawn to Trump because of his economic message, too. “The promise of an easier adulthood for people like me just starting out was very appealing,” she tells the The i Paper.

Leugers, who grew up in a devout conservative Baptist household in Overland Park, a suburb of Kansas City, where Fox News was constantly on the TV, also liked the President’s bluntness. “I had a lot of friends who said, he calls it like it is,” she says. “Some people like how harsh and brash he was. He was ‘meme-able’, they think he’s funny. Some of my friends ate up the YMCA dance he does.”

Memories of the 2008 global financial crisis were still in Leugers’ mind in 2020 when, having just turned 18, she cast her vote for Trump amid the downturn caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. “He campaigned on lowering prices and people my age were getting out of high school, still working low-income jobs just trying to get by,” she says. “A lot of it was on affordability at a time we were trying to make a life for ourselves.”

At the time, Leugers was extremely pro-Maga, having watched countless hours of right-wing influencers on social media. Leugers’ views on Trump began to change during Covid when he made bizarre claims that people should inject themselves with bleach. Leugers was an essential worker with a job in a grocery store.

After the 2024 election, she was dismayed by Trump’s response to the Epstein files, which she saw as a distraction from his failings on Iran, China, ICE raids and Venezuela. As she continued to re-evaluate her beliefs, Leugers moved to Hawaii three months ago, where she now works as a behaviour technician in a clinic for autistic children.

“Trump said to us: ‘We’ll set you up for a successful future,'” she says. “We spent four years waiting and everything got harder and harder. Now diesel is over $7 a gallon. What are we doing?”

Steve Vilchez performed a similarly sharp U-turn on the President. The 22-year-old son of Mexican immigrants grew up on the North Side of Chicago. Vilchez admits that he was drawn to Trump’s brashness. He was 12 when Trump was first elected and said he was initially nervous about the 2016 presidency, but became “captivated” by conservative influencers like the late Charlie Kirk. By 2017, Vilchez was what he calls a “pretty hardcore Donald Trump supporter”.

“I like how he was very confident in himself,” he says. “Even when the experts were telling him he could do something wrong, the way he was defiant, believing he was right, that level of self assurance I really enjoyed.”

Vilchez, who is now a student biology teacher, began to have doubts about Trump due to his response to Covid and the insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January, 2021. Vilchez’s view has further soured since the President took office for a second time and now he considers him a “very dangerous person”.

“It seems like a lot of Trump voters are having a lot of buyer’s remorse,” he says. “The economy is shambles, grocery prices are insane, they’re getting the message Donald Trump lied to them.

“But will they vote Democrat? I haven’t seen a lot of people saying they will do that. People are upset with the Republicans, people are dissatisfied with the Democratic Party, there’s no good option. Everyone’s just scrambling.”Others feel that the damage caused by Trump could turn an entire generation off voting Republican.

Tina Tang, director of polling and analytics at polling company Navigator, said that their research into Gen Z showed a significant number of young voters wished they could take back their vote in 2024.During their last survey of younger voters, Navigator asked what grade they would give the President and most people gave him Ds and Cs, but some gave Trump an F.

“Remember what it’s like being in school and getting a grade like that,” Tang said. “It’s hard to bring it back to an A”.
